I understand that two or three hundred men in the Government shops at Sorel ha\re declared a strike and that the Government have decided to close the shops for a fortnight. May I ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether any arrangement has been arrived at?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We had some trouble there, but I am glad to say that the shops are now open and that work has been resumed.

What arrangements
were made with the strikers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The. men have all gone
back to work.
At the same pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are considering the question of pay. We have granted increases in certain cases where increases were deemed right and proper. As a matter of fact, the matter was being considered 
when the men took the ill-advised step of striking.

It is necessary, I assume, that those vessels should use more than one Canadian port. Can the right hon. Prime Minister inform the llouse whether any action has been taken in the matter? '

Will those' steamers be
constructed in Canada and will they be built of steel or of wood?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When they come to be constructed, they will be constructed in Canada and they will be built of wood. The Quadra was lost in collision, and we find that we can do very much better by building two smaller vessels than by. building one large vessel. We have managed to get along in the meantime by chartering a vessel, and in view of existing conditions, it is not likely we shall proceed with the construction of those vessels this year. That is a matter for consideration.

Has the minister any
intimation to make in regard to the building of wooden vessels in eastern Canada. Early in this session we had an intimation from the Minister of Finance that the Government was giving some consideration to the question of constructing wooden vessels, and I think my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries rather held out the hope that an announcement on the subject might be made in the not distant future; but to my surprise, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a few days ago, made the statement that the Government was not building and did not purpose building any wooden vessels in Canada. I am sure that statement will be a disappointment to a great many in eastern Canada

who would like to see the question of building wooden ships actually taken up by the Government.
In this connection, I would also like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that I am informed that the Imperial Munitions Board, limiting, as they have done, )o 2,500 tons the size of wooden vessels which they are having built for the Imperial Government, are discouraging people in the Maritime Provinces and in other parts of eastern Canada from the idea of utilizing timber from British Columbia, which timber, as the minister knows, is necessary for the construction of larger vessels. The ground on which that is based is, I believe, , that it would be difficult to supply transportation for British Columbia lumber to eastern Canada. I am not sure whether the Imperial Munitions Board, in making that statement, has been influenced at all by the extraordinary action of the minister of Railways in taking up the heavy rails on the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Of course, the taking up of those rails and the substitution of lighter rails would very considerably interfere with the facilities for the transportation of heavy material at low rates of freight over the Transcontinental road. I would have thought that the Imperial Munitions Board and this Government would be disposed to encourage the bringing of British Columbia timber for use in the shipyards of eastern Canada, and I was very much surprised to learn that the Imperial Munitions Board had taken the action they did. There is, however, in eastern Canada, plenty of material for the building of wooden vessels of smaller size, and it might be desirable to have those two vessels built at once so that something may be done in the way of establishing shipbuilding in eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Those vessels are for use on the Pacific coast. The Quadra, which they will replace, was used on the Pacific coast in connection with the Marine Department.

If those two vessels were constructed in eastern Canada, they could be taken 'to British Columbia via the Panama canal. Perhaps this is a good time to ask my hon. friend if anything has resulted from his suggestion to the representatives of the British Government that they should engage in the building of smaller vessels. Only the day before yesterday, at a branch meeting of the Manufacturers' Association, held in the city of St. John, the matter of building smaller wooden vessels
came up, and very strong feeling was expressed in favour of the Government taking up the matter of building wooden vessels. Such vessels are very much required, as my hon. friend will agree. It is almost impossible to-day to obtain vessels for carrying on the coastal service of Canada, and it is almost impossible to secure vessels to bring anthracite coal from the Pennsylvania mines for use in factories, for heating dwellings, and for general use in the cities of the Maritime Provinces. The question is becoming a very serious one, and I would like to hear from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether any steps have been or are likely to be taken by the Government to engage as a Government operation-I do not mean by encouraging private individuals-in the building of smaller wooden vessels in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My information is not exactly the. same as that of my hon. friend. I understand that the reason why the Imperial Munitions Board is not prepared to place contracts for wooden vessels of less than 2,500 tons is because that board has absolute instructions on that point from the British Government, and the vessels which the British Government wish are limited to 2,500 tons, and they are not, up to the present time, willing to authorize the building for them of smaller vessels. That is a policy, of course, which they have to determine; they are the owners of the vessels; it is for them that the vessels are being built; it is for them to declare what sort of vessels they require, and they have declared that at the present time they do not want vessels of less than 2,500 tons. The junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) stated the other night in this House that vessels of that size could not be built in the Maritime Provinces, because it was impossible to secure the lumber to build such vessels. I took the occasion of communicating this. statement both to the Colonial Secretary and to the Director of Shipping, Sir Joseph MacLay, pointing out that I trusted that they would reconsider the matter, and that in the public interest they would see whether or not vessels of a smaller size were desirable for their purposes, and, if they were, that orders would be placed in Canada for their construction. I have not received an answer to that communication yet. The question, of course, has to be decided by the British Government, through the Imperial Munitions Board. There are being constructed in the province of Nova Scotia at the present time

by private individuals 48 wooden vessels, the builders believing that there will be a good margin of profit on vessels of that sort, and that it will prove a profitable undertaking. The information I got by letter was to the effect that the vessels were from 1,500 tons down to about 100 tons. The junior mentber for Halifax, however, said that he did not think any vessels were being constructed in the province as large as 1,500 tons. He said that the largest under construction in the province would be ho more than 1,000 tons, and I think he even mentioned 600 tons. If that is the case, the information that was sent to me by a gentleman who I thought was very well informed as to conditions in Nova Scotia, must be erroneous.
The junior member for Halifax pointed out the very great difficulty there would be in building large wooden ships in the lower provinces on account of the difficulty in getting timber. Still, there is considerable activity in shipbuilding in Nova Scotia, as is evidenced by the 48 vessels now under construction. From the information I have received-and the hon. member for Halifax agrees with me-there is no need to give a bonus to encourage the construction of wooden vessels; the junior member for Halifax expressed the opinion that it was neither desirable nor necessary. The reason is that these vessels can be built and operated at a very substantial profit, providing they escape the submarines and mines, on account of the high freight rates.
The question of building ships in this country for use after the war, to be owned by this Government, is a very important one. Hon. gentlemen will, of course, understand that it would involve the expenditure of a very large sum of money, and at the present time when such very large sums have to be raised for the purpose of carrying on the war, the question of raising additional millions would cause the Finance Minister of this country a great deal of concern; it is a policy that cannot rashly be undertaken, 'but will require the most careful consideration. If private individuals are willing to go into the building of ships of this sort, the Government would not be justified, I think, in entering into competition with them. One of the difficulties in the past about private individuals entering into the building of ships in this country has been the danger of having the ships, after they were completed, commandeered for war purposes, and if commandeered by the British Government they would not earn the ordinary commercial rates, but
[Mr. Hazen.l
what are known as approved rates, which have been fixed by a special committee in England and which are not as high as the ship could earn under private ownership. These are all matters of importance and require the most careful consideration. I have not the statement with me that my hon. friend asked for with, regard to the number of vessels being built in Canada for the Brjtish Government through contracts placed by the Munitions Board, but it has been sent to my office, and I think I shall be able to let my hon. friend have it to-morrow.

I have listened with a very great deal of interest to the statement of my hon. friend and I am sorry that he holds out no hope of assistance to the ship building industry, which would mean the development of a Canadian mercantile marine. My hon. friend tells us that the Imperial Government has made arrangements through the Munitions Board for the construction of large ships, which, when constructed, will be under the control of the Imperial Government, and will not be available for our internal trade. The question of adding to the very few ships in Canada capable of looking after the transportation of our products on the sea is to be left over until after the war. That is not a very hopeful outlook. The minister will remember that the hon. member for St. John last year, and two years ago, and on several occasions since, has urged on the Government the absolute necessity of taking some action in this matter, and it is, indeed, disappointing, after all this discussion, to find that the Government have reached the determination to do nothing whatever towards the creation of a Canadian mercantile marine.
The situation in regard to our internal trade is a very serious one. The question of coal, for instance, and how the people of Canada are to be warmed next winter is a very serious problem indeed. At this moment we are absolutely dependent upon what coal we can get from the United States, and there the direct control of the production and output of the American" collieries is under the American Government, along lines, which, in the judgment of men connected with the coal trade, creates a condition which the people of this country, having regard to the situation in western Canada, can only view with misgiving and alarm. So far as eastern Canada is concerned, to the great distributing point of Montreal there has always been sent a large

quantity of coal, running from 3,000,000 to 4,000,000 tons, but this year practically no coal whatever can he sent along the ordinary channels, not because the coal is not there, for in a great many cases it is lying in the bank, but because of the lack of transportation facilities by water. Practically every collier that was engaged in transporting coal from Nova Scotia to the central part of Canada has been commandeered by the British Government, and the result is, as every business man knows, that the prospects of getting coal by sea from eastern Canada are very, very poor, indeed. The only hope is .that the Minister of Railways will deal with the situation by providing a very low freight rate on the railways, but every one will realize that that will not be at all equal to the transportation of coal by water. That is the condition with regard to coal, which is a very important item to the people of Canada. If the British Government, through the Imperial Munitions Board, commandeer our ships for war purposes, where are we going to get the necessary transportation facilities? The minister tells us that 48 vessels are being built in the province of Nova Scotia. Those may or may not be commandeered; they may be sold to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
I saw by the papers that one was sold only a few days ago.

Of course, the Minister f>f Marine, under the plenary powers given him by the War Measures Act can control the disposition of these vessels. All the small vessels available will be needed to meet the local requirements along our own coast, and if all are of the small character indicated by him they will not supply the needs of the c.ountry for transportation covering greater distances. It seems to me the Government ought to take steps to provide for the construction of vessels. Let these vessels be constructed either by the Government direct pr by private parties, under subvention or in some other way. The means to be taken should be the subject of consideration by the best technical experts who should advise the country how to deal with this very serious problem. I have made some inquiries myself, and, for one thing, I am advised that the statement made that it is impossible to get the plates for the construction of steel vessels is not an accurate statement. That is the advice I received from those to whose .opinions in these matters great weight should be given. Against that advice I would not believe the
statement that has been made without evidence of a most indisputable character. We cannot accept the dictum of an hon. gentleman who happens to think thus and so, when we have statements to the contrary from men engaged in the business.
One of the great mistakes we have made in regard to problems such as this is to accept the statement: You cannot do this, it will take too Jong. We have been saying that in regard to everything material to the welfare of Canada since the war began; and the time has arrived when we must face these problems and must mature a proper, sensible programme in regard to the whole situation. We have been hoping for an early end of the war, and now the conditions facing us are serious enough. It is a question whether we aTe not now too late, but certainly we are getting nearer every day to the time when it will be too late. The best way to avoid being too late is to start now. Transportation conditions in this country demand most radical action. It will not do to leave this problem to be settled after the war. If you cannot have the ships ready in 6ix months, then lay down a programme to have them ready next spring. The days for the production of wooden ships have not gone by; and every one knows that if a programme were laid down now, before next spring we .could place upon the ocean ready for service a huge number of these wooden vessels. And every one of them will be needed, no matter how many you supply. I was told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) ten days ago that every shipyard that could build wooden ships is busy building ships for the Imperial Munitions Board. Yet only two days ago I had a letter from a shipbuilder in my own country in which he'told me he was trying to get a contract for a wooden ship, and if he got the contract he would start building at once, but he had not been able to get the contract up to that time. I see by the press that a firm in Sherbrooke have received a contract'for supplying engines and other material to provide poweT for certain scows now under construction. These must be for vessels of a less capacity than the minimum of the wooden ships to be built under the authority of the Imperial Munitions Board. So much for wooden ships.
Now, in regard to steel ships, the House ought to know authoritatively, whether or not the Government have made inquiries in the United States and Great Britain,

and whether they have information of a definite character as to the production of steel plates. It is manifest that we ought to -build eteel ships if we can, because the same appliances, such as machinery, now being placed in wooden vessels will be of much greater value, as giving more permanent results, if placed in steel ships. Having regard to the great interests at stake, the Government should at once take action for the providing of a mercantile marine, and not leave -this problem until after the war for settlement. We are now entering upon our summer season, and, even if we cannot have ships ready for the autumn, we ought at least to have entered upon a definite certain programme which will enable us to know that these vessels will be built, either of wood or of steel, so that when the season of 1918 opens we shall have ships enough to meet our transportation needs. The coal problem, I warn the minister and the Government, is at this moment so serious that the question may face us, for the first time in our history, of the possibility of Canada being compelled to rely solely on her own products which cannot be transported. This may result in conditions of the greatest possible hardship unless every effort is made to provide means of transport for the coal that is needed. The problem is to use coal from the ports of Nova Scotia near the points of production as a factor in helping to keep warm in winter the people of central Canada, and this problem is so allied with the question of shipping that the need for action on the line I have suggested becomes so great that it must not be disregarded.
Are the ships that are being ordered by the Munitions Board wholly of wood?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Many of them are steel ships.
Will the Board accept a ship built wholly of wood?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that they will, if the ship is not less than 2,500 tons.
It is not necessary that the frame be steel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that it is not necessary.
What kind of wood is used?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
British Columbia fir and pine, I understand.
C!Ar. Macdonald.]

I am sure there are
many people who would like to get that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sure the Munitions Board would be delighted to give it.

The Munitions Board do not encourage the building of ships in Eastern Canada in which British Columbia timber is to be used. Some one has told them that the timber cannot be transported. But if the Transcontinental Railway were given the order, I am sure they would be able to transport enough timber to build many ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not here to represent the Munitions Board, but I should like to know what authority the hon. gentleman has for his statement.

I have been told directly that the Board discourages giving contracts to persons who contemplate bringing their timber from British Columbia. I have a letter to that effect. I either have a letter or a gentleman who went to the Munitions Board with a view of getting a contract stated that that was represented to him; but I am inclined to think that I have a letter myself to the same effect.
Of course, the unjustifiable dismantling of the Transcontinental railway by the Minister of Railways and Canals may be a reason for lack of transportation facilities, but in northern British Columbia, in the Prince Rupert district, we know there are vast foresit areas where long timber can be got in enormous quantities and which might be easily hauled over the Transcontinental railway for use in the shipyards of eastern Canada. Let me ask the minister if he will not see the Munitions Board and find out what the exact position of the matter is. If the minister will inquire of the Munitions Board he will find, I am sure, that that is the view which the Board take and that they discourage people from taking contracts to build wooden ships of 2,500 tons if they are relying on British Columbia timber. They speak of the difficulties of transportation. It was said here recently-
I think yesterday-that the Transcontinental railway is not doing very much business in western Canada, and especially through the mountains. I do not know whether that is true or not, hut if it is taue, why should not that road he utilized to transport timber to the shipyards of eastern Canada where it may be used for the building of wooden ships?

Now, I will leave that question and I will take up what my hon. friend says in regard to the building of wooden vessels by the Canadian Government. Even at the risk of some foolish person, or some foolish newspaper, outside of the House saying that I am interfering with the carrying on of the war because I criticise the Government, I desire to say that the Government has not discharged its duty to the people of this country in not having long ago engaged in the building of wooden ships. It is not discharging its duty to-day in determining, as it was announced here that it had determined, that it will do nothing in that direction., My hon. friend speaks of vessels being built in the shipyards of Nova Scotia by private 'parties at their awn expense. Why should the shipbuilders of eastern Canada be placed at a disadvantage by toeing obliged to finance the enterprise entirely themselves while tbe builders of steel ships in British Columbia are assisted by the Imperial Government or the Imperial Munitions Board? Is this Government afraid to do what the British Government is doing? Is this Government afraid to engage in the building of vessels when the British Government is doing so? When the United States entered into the war, the United States Government immediately appropriated 150,000,000 for the purpose of building wooden vessels. They did not require that they should be of 2,500 tons. They ordered that there should be a thousand wooden vessels constructed of a capacity of 1,000 tons each. That was the order which' the United States gave to the proper officials-I think Mr. Goethels is the chairman of the United States ship construction board.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend must have seen that they are not going to build them now.

I have not seen it. I suppose they are not going to build them because they have great opportunities for building steel vessels. My hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) has pictured the condition of the people in consequence of the high cost of transportation applying to fuel, foodstuffs, and everything which the people require, the cost of which is becoming so great that a condition of misery and almost of starvation has been created and there is danger almost of people freezing to death in some parts of this country. That might be prevented toy the Government doing something with regard to the question of transportation . .Why are they
not doing it? My hon. friend says that they are going to do it after the war. After the war there will be no necessity for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not say so.

I thought the hon. gentleman said that after the war this would be a very important question to be considered. His colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), during the present session, said that he was utilizing his staff for the purpose of working out a scheme to engage in the building of ships after the war. It is not after the war that the people require such relief. It is now. It was two years ago, it was nearly three years ago that the Government ought to have taken the matter up. It is with regret that I do it, but I do make the charge that this Government has with respect to the building of wooden ships absolutely failed in the duty which it owes to the Canadian people. Our boys who are at the front have left their mothers and sisters in Canada. There are certain provisions made for them but if the cost of fuel and the cost of the necessaries of life goes up by leaps and bounds as it has been going up for months and months past it is going to render the condition of this class of the community, as well' as of all the other people in Canada who are not possessed of very large means, very deplorable. Take the city of St. John in which my hon. friend lives when he is in his home town and to-day our people are paying $14 per ton for anthracite coal and the word I get from there is that the dealers refuse to enter into a contract because they do not know how they will be able to get their coal from the mines in Pennsylvania to St. John. Is that not a condition which ought to excite attention on the part of hon. gentlemen? Do they turn deaf ears to the appeals which are going out from the people in this particular?
How is the Government going to deal with it? It is the same all through Ontario.

By building vessels and bringing rates down to a fair and reasonable charge. That is the way the Government is going to do it. I do not assume that if the Government do build vessels and engage in transportation they are going to keep the prices away up the same as the speculators keep them up. I do not imagine that if the Government were to take charge of the flour mills of Canada they would charge the same extravagant rates for the manufacture of flour as the private miller is doing. I would assume that if the Gov-

ernment built vessels they -would give relief to the people in the way of transportation and keep the charges down to within reasonable limits. As far as coal and many other of the necessaries of life are concerned, it is the high cost of transportation that is increasing the prices to these exorbitant iamounts, and which are imposing such burdens on the people to-day.
Freight rates are under the control of a commission, are they not?
No, not on vessels.
But they are on railways?	'

My hon. friend ought to know that transportation by water ought to be very much cheaper than transportation by rail, and yet to-day you cannot get transportation by water (between the producing districts in the United States, where coal is mined, and - mined in abundance, and the ports of the Maritime Provinces. Or, if the Government were to go into the building of vessels they would he able to place these vessels on the routes where they were most required and by charging fair and reasonable rates they would be able to keep down the cost of transportation and so give relief to the people who are, as I have said, in a very distressing condition to-day in many sections of the country, and whose condition will be deplorable in the near future if nothing is done by the Government for their relief. However, I have discharged my duty and it rests with the Government to say whether they will do anything or whether they will continue the do-nothing policy which they have pursued in this regard ever since the war began. My hon. friend says it would take money to build wooden vessels. But did not his colleague the Minister of Railways (Mr. Qochrane) only yesterday introduce a Bill which will authorize him to expend $10,000,000 of the money of the people of this country on the construction of highways, which are not needed in these times of waT? What the Government ought to do is to take that $10,000,000 and build wooden vessels to assist in cheapening transportation at once and give relief to the people of this country in the direction in which relief is most needed. Let the construction of highways, which, after all, are largely for the use of the automobilists of this country, wait; these matters of necessity may well stand over until the settling of the war. Let the Government devote what m.oney they have to what really can be accomplished

for the purpose of relieving distress, and distress in many particulars can be best relieved by decreasing the cost of transportation in Canada.

When I saw in the newspapers that the Munitions Board were giving contracts in British Columbia for the construction of wooden ships, I went down to the Munitions Board and asked one of the officials if contracts would toe given in eastern Canada, and he told me that so soon as the men who are conducting the business for the board in British Columbia and the West were through with their business in that part of Canada, they would proceed to the Maritime Provinces. I was informed that any person who would assure the board that he had a proper shipyard, properly equipped, and had competent men in charge of it, would be given contracts for 2,500-ton wooden ships.

Nothing less than 2,500
tons.

He said 2,500-ton
wooden steamships. This information was given freely to me, and I do not think there i3 any secret about it.
Did the hon. member ask if any less than that tonnage would be constructed?

That is what I was told, that the ships were all of a standard tonnage of 2,500 tons. . I do not think that, as the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) has stated, the building of these ships is to be confined to British Columbia. I have applied to menin my own province and asked them to consider the matter and find out what quantities of wood were
4 p.m. available there for the building of ships, and I am assured that, with the exception of certain portions of the ship, wood is available in the three Maritime Provinces.

What I said was that to build these 2,500-ton ships in eastern Canada it would in most cases be necessary to bring timber from British Columbia, and while the Munitions Board would give contracts to build in eastern Canada, they would discourage the entering into contracts involving the bringing of timber from British Columbia. They put forward the difficulty of transportation. That is what I understood.
I do not see why the hon. member should wish the board to discourage the building of ships in eastern Canada.

The hon. member insists on misunderstanding me. They will discourage the building of wooden ships in eastern Canada if the builders wish to depend for their timber, or any portion of it, on British Columbia. That is what I said.
I do not think they will depend on British Columbia to get lumber.
For the large vessels they say they must.

There is a sufficient quantity of lumber in eastern Canada, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to build the ships, and I have no doubt that these gentlemen on their return from the West will offer contracts.

A gentleman was here the other day from New Brunswick who has facilities for shipbuilding in a portion of New Brunswick, the north shore, which is perhaps the best timbered section in the province. He was prepared to engage at once in the building of four wooden ships of a tonnage not exceeding 500 tons each. He said if he had to build larger vessels than that, up to the specifications of the Munitions Board, he would be obliged to procure a portion of the timber from British Columbia.

Why not from the
Southern States?
That might be done, of course.

I have given the
information which I received, and that information is that contracts will be offered after these gentlemen return from British Columbia. The Imperial Government will supply and pay for all materials for the construction of these ships, and give a fair profit, but the profit for eastern Canada has not yet been settled.

Is there a uniform
price?

I do not know. I
did not inquire, but I suppose it will depend upon the local markets what they will pay for lumber in different sections.

Is there a standard
model or pattern of ship?

The hon. member can get that information at the Munitions Board; I did not go into it very particularly. I just wanted to know whether the information which was given in this House and the statements made in this House that the Munitions Board would not construct in the East were true or not, and I found out that they were not true, that the Board intended to offer contracts in the East.
Did they intimate when that would take place?
So soon as the gentlemen conducting this business returned from the West.

Who was the official
whom the hon. gentleman saw?

If my hon. friend
will consult Mr. Fitzgerald he will get the information which I received.

I .desire to point out the
situation in Nova Scotia with respect to the securing of a supply of anthracite coal for which provision will have to be made in the course of' a few months. It appears to be almost impossible to get tonnage to convey this coal from Boston or New York to ports in Nova Scotia. Soane ten days ago; I think rates as high as $8 a ton were being offered in Boston for the carriage of anthracite coal from that port to ports in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. One can readily see that the imposition of such a charge as that for transportation would render it almost impossible for the ordinary consumer of anthracite to lay in a supply for the approaching winter season. The same condition obtains with regard to the carriage of soft coal. I know that in the island of Cape Breton large collieries are obliged to bank great quantities of coal that should be in course of transportation to the different places where local consumption of coal is necessary and where the supply of coal is very much shorter than it would ordinarily be at this season of the year. I do not know what immediate steps the Government can take to relieve this situation. I believe the conditions existing in the island of Cape Breton as regards the shipment of coal from Those mines to other parts of the Maritime Provinces is due to the fact that the Government has commandeered a large number of steamers and has taken many vessels out of the carrying trade.
I regret very much that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries does not seem to be able to find a solution of the difficulty. Not only are the consumers of coal hampered

by reason of the enormous freights being charged, but the produceis as well are hampered by reason of their inability to get shipment for their coal to different points in the Maritime Provinces. There are ample facilities in the province of Nova Scotia for the construction of smaller ships than those to which reference has been made by the minister, and a large number of wooden ships would now be in course of construction in that province if some kind of encouragement had been given. The member for St. John has referred to the enormous expenditure proposed by the Minister of Railways and Canals under the Bill introduced yesterday. I agree with the hon. member for St. John that the expenditure of $10,000,000 for the improvement of highways at this time is absolutely unjustifiable and indefensible, having regard to the crying need for more vessels to carry coal and other necessaries of life from the different ports of the Maritime Provinces. Certainly the Government cannot refuse to take action upon the plea that money is not available.
Why was coal not carried to the lake regions by means of vessels before the war?
I know of no other way of carrying it up to the lakes-although a few years ago the member for West Peterborough was advocating the use of flying machines for transportation purposes.

We are stuck for coal in Ontario, but' they do not think of bringing it to this part of the country by means of vessels. It is said that coal cannot be cheaply carried that way, partly owing to inability to control the mines and operators. The result has been the high price of coal in Ontario-and it seems likely to continue. When it was suggested that the railways were overcharging, it was found that that was not the case.

My information is that the people of Ontario pay less for bringing coal all the way from the Pennsylvania mines by rail than the people of the Maritime Provinces are obliged to pay for bringing it by water. Transportation by water ought not to be one-quarter as expensive as transportation by rail.
Then why have vessels not been used in the past for this purpose?

Because there have been so few vessels.
fMr. Kyte.l

Before the war there was no scarcity of vessels for the transportation of coal, but since the commencement of war the Government have commandeered a number of vessels that were previously engaged in that work. Coal has not, I think, been at any time carried from Nova Scotia to the Great Lakes by vessels, because the vessels were unable to pass through the canals. So far as our tonnage in the Maritime Provinces is concerned, therefore, conditions affecting the transport of coal to the lakes are not different now from what they were a few years ago. It is in the highest degree desirable that some active steps should at once be taken to relieve the present condition of affairs. This is the season of the year when hard coal is being purchased and held in stock for next winter, but the people of the Maritime Provinces are unable to lay in their supply of coal at this season, and thus take advantage of the reduced price, because of the prohibitive rates charged as a result of the scarcity of tonnage.

I wish to read a letter which I received from the Director of Steel Shipbuilding in answer to a communication which I wrote to the Munitions Board asking for information as to the standard of vessels. I did that because some gentlemen in New Brunswick were desirous of engaging in shipbuilding. This letter, which is not of a private nature, puts the Board's position very clearly. It is as follows:
May 16, 1917.
Wm. Pugsley, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
City.
Dear Sir.-
In reply to your letter of May 15th.
The Board has been authorized by the British Ministry of Shipping to arrange for the construction of a certain number of wooden ships in Canada according to a standard type. The design and specifications can be seen at any time at the Board's office.
The vessels are of approximately 2,500 tons deadweight, being 250 feet long, 40 feet in beam and 21 feet draft.
The terms on which the Board is placing these contracts are the reimbursement of the contractor for the actual cost of building, including labour, material and overhead, plus a fixed sum by way of profit for each vessel constructed. Under these circumstances, and because definite results must be secured, the Board will examine closely into the capacity, resources and experience of each firm seeking a contract.
With regard to the plant, etc., employed, in the construction, individual arrangements will be made in each case on the basis of allowing a reasonable amortization as part of the cost of construction, or in the case of an existing plant allowing a reasonable rental for the use of the plant as part of the cost.

With regard to any construction undertaken in Eastern Canada, the essential point will be for the contractor to satisfy the Board thajt he has or can obtain on reasonable terms a sufficient quantity of suitable lumber to build the type of ship required. It is not safe to reckon on obtaining lumber from British Columbia ; firstly, because we expect that most of the lumber suitable for the purpose, which is cut there, will be taken up in wooden ship construction on the Pacific coast, and secondly because it is doubtful whether any large quantity of lumber could be brought across the continent in the present railway situation even if it were available.
You are quite at liberty to communicate the above information to your friends, and the Board will be very glad to' give more detailed information to any one interested.
Yours truly,
William I. Gear, Director of Steel Shipbuilding.
I was struck by the statement in the latter part of the letter that it is doubtful whether any large quantity of lumber could be brought across the continent, having regard to the present railway situation, even if the lumber were available. A gentleman who was desirous of forming a company to engage in shipbuilding told me that he had been informed by the Board that they would not give him a contract if he had to rely on British Columbia lumber. It ought to be possible for the Government to have lumber from northern British Columbia and the vicinity of Prince Rupert, where, I am told, there is an abundant supply, brought over the Transcontinental railway and used in the shipyards of eastern Canada.
Just a day or two ago I had a letter from a gentleman at Diligent river, Nova Scotia. He stated that he had a shipyard where wooden vessels could be built in large numbers, and that he would be very glad to place it, I think he said, free of charge, at the disposal of this Government for the purpose of building ships. My hon. friend knows that in the harlbour of St. John, in the vicinity of St. John, along the Kenne-becasis river, along the St. John river, at St. Martin's, at St. Andrew's and at St. George, at other places on the Bay of Fundy coast, at Richibucto, on the Mir-amiehi river, at Bathurst, at Campellton, along the Baie des Chaleurs coast, along the 'St. Lawrence, there are thousands of opportunities for building wooden vessel's, and at these places wooden shipbuilding was carried on in the past on a large scale. I wish to repeat what I said, that I think the Government ought to let contracts for the building of small wooden vessels of say 500 tons capacity, and to take measures, where it is necessary to bring timber from
British Columbia, to have it brought east in enormous quantities for the purpose of assisting in the construction of wooden vessels. There are large quantities of timber in eastern Canada, but I think, to build larger vessels with southern -pine or British Columbia timber would in most cases be required, and there is the same difficulty of getting southern pine to the Maritime Provinces as there is in getting coal carried, because it would have to be brought by water, but British Columbia timber, whenever it is required to be mixed with eastern timber, could be brought by the Government over the Transcontinental. Let the Government act and they will receive the enthusiastic approval of the members of this House and of the people of this country. Let them start in, as the United States Government hag done, as the British Government has done, to build ships to assist in transportation, and they will be conferring an enormous benefit upon the people, and I am sure that if they will, even at this late hour, engage in this most important work, they will receive the approval of the people of Canada.

I would not like this item to pass without saying a word on behalf of the mother province of the Dominion. There was a time when the province of Quebec shared in the glories of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in the building of wooden ships which covered the seven seas, and when Canada ranked as the fifth greatest shipbuilding nation in the world. I read to-day in the Montreal Gazette that the tonnage passing through the Lachine canal has decreased considerably since last year, and almost daily our inland tonnage is falling off. All the arguments that have been advanced on behalf of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick apply with ten times as much force to the St. Lawrence, because the St. Lawrence is the main artery of this country, and on the St. Lawrence, in the old province of Quebec, we have the largest city of Canada, which consumes more coal than any other Canadian city, and where last winter we had a coal shortage which was a very serious problem, and which problem is going to be ten times worse during next winter unless the Government wake up and do something. One of the clever moves which paved the way for a change in the administration of this country was when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce brought forward the idea of the creation of a Canadian navy, and ultimately the encouragement of shipbuilding in Canada. That was the starting point

which led the then Opposition on to the road which ultimately (brought them into office. It was the .policy of the Opposition of that day to encourage shipbuilding. Last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself, if my memory does not fail me, advocated strongly the construction of ships in this country, and it stands to reason that Canada will never take the position which she should hold amongst the nations of the world unless she goes extensively into the building of ships. We have built hundreds and thousands of miles of railway throughout Canada; we have opened up every part of the country; we have given access to all our various industries, our mines, our fisheries, our lumber, but our domain ends when we r'each the water's edge. We have not yet got properly on to the water; we are trusting to England and to foreign countries to carry our goods across the ocean. The number of ships on the Canadian register is practically nil and is growing smaller and smaller every day. Our inland tonnage is doing practically nothing. We hear some complaints-
Mi*. W. H. BENNETT: Is the hon. member aware that last year a boat was launched at Collingwood capable of carrying a million bushels of grain?
I will give Collingwood credit for launching one boat last year.
There are a large number on the stocks.

We were informed the other evening by the Minister of Finance that by an Order in Council recently passed a shipbuilder gets a rebate of all the duty he has paid on materials entering into the construction of a ship. It is similar to the law in regard to agricultural implements, boilers and other manufactured goods. If you import boiler plates from the United States, and construct a boiler in Canada and then export it to some other country, you get a rebate of 99 per cent of the customs duties paid on the materials used in the construction of the boiler. If it is true that this rebate is now granted in regard to the shipbuilding industry, it is a step in the right direction. Prior to this Order in Council, a certain number of articles entering into the construction of ships were on the free list, such as plates and other articles that could not be made in Canada. I was led to believe in the discussion the other evening that the duty would be rebated on all articles entering
into the construction of a ship, and I should like to know if that covers material that is manufactured in Canada. For instance, if I am building a steel vessel in Nova Scotia I naturally go to Dartmouth for rivets. The manufacturer in Dartmouth takes advantage of the tariff, and charges 27 per cent or whatever the protection is on rivets. Under the Order in Council, would I get that duty rebated, just as if the rivets had been imported from the United States or some other country?

I was not aware that we
would have a discussion of this sort when my Estimates came up to-day, or I would have had more information on this subject.
I think that my hon. friend from Bona-venture, who always speaks eloquently and in a way that is pleasant to hear, is better informed on other matters than on the subject he discussed here this afternoon. He spoke as though little or nothing were being done in the building of large ships in the province of Quebec. He said that some small construction work was being done at the Vickers works in Montreal. It may surprise my hon. friend to learn that there are under construction at the Vickers works in Montreal six cargo steam-, ers of 7,000 tons each. Other vessels are also being constructed at that yard, one of 2,360 tons, and others of less tonnage. The shipyard employs over 2,000 men and keeps them as busy as possible. At the Davie Shipbuilding Yards, Levis, there is a vessel of 5,000 tons being constructed. At Sorel, in certain private shipyards, there is a great amount of activity in shipbuilding. Almost within sight of the city of Quebec, on the Island of Orleans, a company with which Mr. Playfair, who is known to hon. members in connection with shipping on the Great Lakes, is connected, is building four wooden ships of from 1,500 to 2,000 tons, and I am informed that a large portion of the lumber entering into the construction of these ships is being brought from British Columbia. Further, I may say that a gentleman was here to-day who is largely engaged in shipbuilding, and he states that he has made arrangements for bringing a large quantity of British Columbia lumber down to points on the St. Lawrence, where he is going to construct some 8 or 10 wooden ships, as large, I presume, as those that are being built on the Island of Orleans, from 1,500 to 2,000 tons each. Two of the ships that are being constructed at the Island of Orleans are well on the way to

completion, and work has been commenced on two others. I think that is an answer to the statement of my hon. friend from St. John that there is great difficulty in getting lumber from British Columbia. Not only is some of the lumber that is going into the construction of these ships being brought from British Columbia, but I am informed that Mr. Norcross has made large purchases of lumber in that province, and is going to build ships of British Columbia lumber and lumber obtained elsewhere.
There are a large number of ships being built at the present time in Canadian shipyards, aggregating a very considerable amount of tonnage. Six are being constructed in the Vickers yard of 7,000 tons each, and I think they are all under way. The Davie Shipbuilding and Bepairing Company, Levis, are building one steel vessel of 5,000 tons. The Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Co., of New Glasgow, N.S., have under construction three cargo steamers of a total tonnage of 6,800. The Shelburne Shipbuilders Company are building a wooden cargo steamer of 320 tons. Robert Rutledge, of Sheet Harbour, N.S., is building a wooden cargo steamer of 325 tons. The Quebec Shipbuilding and Repairing Co., Isle of Orleans, are building two auxiliary schooners of 2,490 tons, and a tug boat is being built at Sorel of 410 tons. In addition, there is a large amount of other construction which I do not care to speak about here, going on at the Sorel shipyards, at the Davie 'Works, Quebec; at Poisons, Toronto; at Canadian Vickers, Montreal, and at other shipyards throughout the country. On the Great Lakes the Port Arthur Shipbuilding and Repairing Go., Limited, are building four cargo steamers aggregating 9,748 tons. The Collingwood Shipbuilding Company are building one steel cargo steamer of 7,988 tons, and two steel oil tankers of 4,800 tons.
The Poison Iron Works, Limited, Toronto, are building two cargo steamers of 4,400 tons each and six cargo steamers of 3,500 tons each, in all eight steamers, in addition to other marine construction work which is going on there. The Thor Iron Works Limited, have two steel cargo steamers on the stocks of 5,000 tons each. The Georgian Bay Shipbuilding and Repairing Company, Midland, Ontario, as pointed out toy my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. W. H. Bennett) recently launched a large steamer there, and other construction is in progress. On the Pacific coast a great deal of shipbuilding is carried on. The Coughlin Com-
[Mr. Hazen.l
pany has a contract for five large steel steamers of 8,800 tons each, and in the Wallace yards two steel vessels of 4,600 tons each are in course of construction. Hon. members will see from these figures that there is a great deal of activity in steel shipbuilding in Canada.
Now, with regard to wo.oden ships, I have here a list of wooden vessels being built at points on the Atlantic coast aside from those that are building under contracts placed by the Munitions Board. This list is complete so far as I know at present. In that connection it may not be uninteresting to call attention to the fact that the British authorities have issued an order excluding sailing vessels from the war area. This step has been taken because of the risk tp which these vessels are exposed from submarines, through their inability to escape. In reaching this decision the authorities are moved I assume, toy the consideration, not only pf loss of vessels, but of the loss of cargoes as well. They have made a request of us to adppt the same policy and to exclude Canadian sailing vessels from the war area.
Does that order apply to sailing vessels with auxiliary power?

speechtext:
It would depend on the price.
, Mr. HAZEN: The question of price was not raised; the price would have been satisfactory. These people said that shipbuilding in the province of New Brunswick had become almost a lost art. It flourished years ago, as the hon. member for Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil) said. In those days there used to be ship carpenters, sail makers, caulkers, and other ship's tradesmen, but these have pretty well disappeared. At any Tate, the parties with whom I communicated could not find any one willing to enter into a contract for the construction of these ships. I say this to show that at present there are difficulties in the way of constructing vessels of large size. This applies especially to New Brunswick. In Nova Scotia shipbuilding has been better maintained, schooners and other vessels have always been built in that province, and that accounts, probably, for the greater shipbuilding activity in Nova Scotia to-day. As I understand it, if there are builders who will build what the British Government requires-and they must be the judge of their own requirements-they will have no difficulty in getting contracts from the Imperial Munitions Board.
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has drawn the attention of the committee to a very serious question in regard to the coal supply of Nova Scotia. It undoubtedly is a very important and serious question. I have had several consultations and interviews with people representing the Dominion Coal Company during the last few days. The Dominion Coal Company has been placed in a rather awkward position. The vessels which the company were using to transport their coal at the time of the outbreak of the war were, with one single exception, British registered vessels and were subject to requisition by the British Government. They had only one vessel which was a Canadian registered vessel. That vessel was also requisitioned by the British Government but I am taking steps to have it released. It will help to some extent to relieve the situation. They find it impossible-it is not a matter of price with them-to charter vessels for the putrevised EDITION

pose of carrying their coal not only to St. John and Halifax but to ports on the St. Lawrence as well. We have discussed the whole matter and we have taken steps which we think will go a long way towards relieving the situation in those two places.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext:
Not by reason of restoring one ship. I have mentioned one step that we have taken but there are other steps that I cannot explain to the House at the present time. But that, one ship will to a considerable extent relieve the situation and it will be an important factor in doing it. In addition to that, the Dominion Coal Company have had large contracts for supplying coal to ports in the United States and they have come to the conclusion that they will have to cancel these contracts and announce to the people in Boston and other places that they will have to look elsewhere for their coal, that their efforts will have to be directed to providing coal for places in Canada under existing circumstances.
These are the principal subjects that were touched on in connection with the discussion here to-day. There is no doubt that there is a greater development of shipbuilding in Canada than the country has known for many years. I believe as a result of what is going on to-day the shipbuilding yards in Canada will be placed in a considerably better position than they have been at any time during the past twenty-five or thirty years. I further believe that when the war is over they will be able to compete on more even terms with the shipbuilders of the United Kingdom. But up to the present time, as I pointed out in this House before, the Canadian shipbuilders have had no protection. British registered ships built in the Old Country have come into our ports to compete with the ships that were built in this country without paying any duty, even upon their equipment and the things that were necessary to enable them to sail their ships. But, there has been an enormous advance in wages in the United Kingdom. My belief is that wages in the United Kingdom, after the war is over, will never get down to the point at which they were before the war and which gave the shipbuilder of the United Kingdom an undue advantage in competition with the shipbuilders in this and otheT countries.

subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext: Will they come down in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext: I do not know that they will. Wages in the United Kingdom are quite as high as they are in Canada and I do not believe they will come down for some years because there will be great activity after the war is over in building ships. The troops will have to be brought back, the munitions and equipment will have to be brought from the front and in consequence of submarine attacks there will be fewer ships than there were at the outbreak of the war. To carry on the business of the world there will be a great demand for ships, in consequence of that the shipyards of Great Britain and Canada will have a great deal of work to do and they will require to build a good many ships for carrying on the business for some years to come. I expect the Canadian shipyards, with the impetus they are getting now, will be able to compete with the shipbuilders of the United Kingdom. You find shipyards with contracts for six and eight large ships and as a result their yards will be better equipped and in a very much better position to compete than they were before.

speechtext:
The American loan has only been made recently. The British Government gave its order for this large amount of tonnage long before the United States made to Great Britain an offer of a portion of its loan. But surely if the British Government has ordered ships built in Canada it ik because the British Government want those ships, it is for the benefit of the Empire. The British Government is having ships built here because it requires them. What I complain of is that this Government is doing nothing. My hon. friend says that the British Government would not have given orders in Canada if it had not been that this Government gave a bredit. Let him put it oh that low ground if he wishes, although I do not believe one word of it. But when the British Government is giving orders to the extent of millions of dollars to the United States, would it not have given orders for the building of ships in Canada unless Canada had agreed to lend some money to it? That is putting it upon a pretty low ground indeed, to >
say that that is the reason which induced the British Government to give orders for the building of ships in Canada.
There is one great advantage which the House and the country will receive from the statement of my hon. friend to-day, and that is that we will get at the facts, because my hon. friend has read a list of ships under construction in Canada. We have had it stated over and 5 p.m. over again by members of the Government, by the Minister of

Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), by the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) that every shipyard in -Canada, every place capable of building ships, was filled with orders, and that there was no opportunity to build any more ships than were being -constructed to-day.
iMr. HAZEN. That is true of every shipyard that builds steel ships.
'Mr. PUGSLEY: Does.not my hon. friend know that for the building of wooden vessels of 500 tons to 1,000 tons it does not take very long to put a shipyard, one that was formerly used, in good repair?' You want a good location, and you can soon get the yard ready. If the Government would give an order for 500 -wooden vessels of 500 'tons each to be built in -Canada, it would soon get offers by the score, offers by the hundred, offers by the thousand, to build those ishijps in eastern -Canada, in Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. But my hon. friend's statement is valuable in another respect; it corrects the statement which he made upon another recent occasion in the House that forty-eight vessels were -being built in the Maritime Provinces, and that the size of the vessels ranged from 1,500 tons down to 150 tons. My hon. friend has read a list to-day and has not mentioned, if I remember aright, a single vessel of a tonnage greater than GOO tons, -and in order to make up his full -list of forty-eight vessels, he puts in a little boat of a capacity of 38 tons, and many of them of 150 tons, little motor boats I suppose they would be. All of this shows the effort which has been made on the other side of the House to mislead the people of this country, to make them believe that there is a vast deal of shipbuilding going on in Canada-r Why, with all that is being done to-day, when ships are demanded not only for the Atlantic and Pacific business, but for the coasting business of Canada, when there is a -demand- -unparalled, such as never existed in this -country before, all the vessels named by my -hon. friend would not -be one-tenth part of the tonnage that was being turned out in the old days of peace when wooden shipbuilding in Canada was at its height. They turned out more ships in the little province of Prince Edward Island, more wooden vessels in number, than all those mentioned by my hon. friend.

subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext:
This is what I said, that this Government is doing nothing to encourage Canadian transportation by water. Has not my hon. friend proved it himself? Every one of those steel ships which is being built, he says, has either 'been -contracted for to be sold to the British Government or to other governments-not one for the Canadian Government. The Government of every other country in the world deems it necessary to build ships to assist in the transportation in which it is immediately concerned. The British Government is buying ships in order to bring food to their own people, food to the armies, food to the Allies. Neutral countries are buying vessels to be built in Canada, but the Canadian Government gives no contract for a single vessel, buys not one single vessel, for the purpose of reducing the cost of transportation for the benefit of the Canadian people. That is why I say that the Canadian Government is doing nothing for the people of Canada. My hon. friend thinks that, because the ships are being built in Canada, that is a great thing for the Canadian people. All it does is to give employment, that is all; in these days, when men are scarce, it gives more employment. It does not reduce the cost of living, it does not reduce the cost of transportation, it does not give people cheaper coal, or cheaper flour, or cheaper foodstuffs of all kinds, which they would obtain if you cheapened the transportation of the country. Does not my hon. friend the minister see that the Governments of almost every other country in the world are either building ships or buying ships to be used for the benefit of their own people, while the Canadian Government stands all alone in absolutely refusing to do anything in this direction, absolutely alone? That is the record which Canada has to-day. My hon. friend has spoken of what is being done in the way of shipbuilding at the Vickers-Maxim plant. I am extremely glad that these shi-ps are being built at the Vickers-Maxim works. The fact that that firm are able to-day to do so much is a tribute to the foresight of the late Liberal Government, which gave the contract which led to the building of the dock an-d the shipbuilding plant near Montreal by the Vickers-Maxim Company, and if it had not been for what we did, giving a contract which I had the honour of signing when I was Minister of Public Works, what would have been the position so far as that portion of Canada is concerned? Not one ship would be in the course of construction in the vicinity of the city of Montreal-not

one. Then take the Collingwood ' plant. That was established under contract with , the late Liberal Government. So was the Poison Iron Works of Toronto, and the Port Arthur Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company, where my hon. friend says they are turning out four ships, that yard was established by the Liberal Government, and I had the honour of turning the first sod in connection with the building of the dry dock and the establishment of the ship repairing plant. Therefore, if it were not for what the Liberal Government had done my hon. friend would not have very much to boast of to-day. And this is what we complain of. We do it as respectfully as we can, we do it with the best feeling it is possible to show.
In the matter of shipbuilding the record of the Government is an absolute blank. My hon. friend talks about the difficulty of getting money, but the Government has millions to spend in the purchase of _ a derelict railway, the Quebec and Saguenay, and, apparently, millions to spend on the construction of highways. Not a dollar, however, is devoted to shipbuilding. My hon. friend will build ships for any country in the world that wants them, but as for building ships for the benefit of the Canadian people-perish the thought! He admits .that the difficulties of the consuming population are very serious. They are more than serious. In many sections of Canada the people look forward to the coming winter with great anxiety because of the fear that they will not be able to get enough coal .to keep their houses warm and avoid suffering and hardship. The prices of all the necessaries of life have gone up tremendously, much more than they would have gone up if the Government had, even in a small way, taken charge of the water transportation of Canada and provided for the building of ships. My hon. friend says that they are suffering hardships in England; that they cannot get potatoes; that *they are living on allowances. Is that any answer to make to the people of a country that is 3,000 miles from the theatre of war, a country which is far richer in proportion to population than any other country in the world? There ought to be no distress in Canada, a country which is capable of producing enormous quantities of foodstuffs, which has an abundance of bituminous coal, and which is . alongside the great coal mines of Pennsylvania. The people are in actual distress because of the high cost of the necessaries of life. My hon. friend, although he admits the condition to
be serious, turns a deaf ear to the appeals which the people, through the members of this- Parliament, are making to him and to his Government to take some steps to secure cheaper transportation. You may theorize as much as you like; the only course for this Government to pursue, if they wish to remedy this condition, is to give contracts for the building of ships and, by taking charge of water transportation, cheapen the cost of carrying the necessaries of life from the point of production to the point of consumption. Why do they not do it? Is it because they have a prejudice against the building of ships? Let me implore them , to remember that it was only warships that they asked the people to believe they could not build in Canada. If they engage in the building of commercial vessels, they will not be regarded as having gone back on their policies. Let them not be afraid to do it; let them take a step which will be more advantageous to the people than anything else that they could do. Parliament would gladly ratify any proposal of that kind and I am sure that the country would be enthusiastic in its support of the Government's action. Indeed, they would almost -but not quite-forget many of the sins of which the Government have been guilty.

subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext:
I assume that they will be used where they will be of most advantage.
- Mr. MARCIL: Having regard to the shipbuilding activity that has taken place in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and along the St. Lawrence without a national shipbuilding policy,-it must be evident to the minister that if the Government gave some sort of encouragement to the industry, it would be very materially extended. What we need is ships to carry the products of the country inland. The first trip of a subsidized steamer last year on the Baie des Chaleurs route to Gasp6 was made on the 5th of August, so that during the months of April, May, June and July not a single ship was available to convey to suitable markets the salmon caught in that vicinity, which are unparalleled in the world. In answer to questions which I asked on two or three occasions last year, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he was unable to get ships. This year he has put on a small river boat which had been hardly sufficient for the business on the St. John river, and which is not at all adequate for the business in whigh it is now engaged. It is unable to handle the trade, and along that whole coast there is practically no shipping whatever. The Baie des Chaleurs, on the Quebec as well as on the New Brunswick side, is one of the finest sheets of water on the North American continent. For tourists it is unsurpassed. There is an ocean trip in view of land, with an ever-changing scenic panorama. The resources of that peninsula have not been touched. There is enough pulpwood there to supply the North American continent for a century, but the Government has made no fttempt whatever to develop those resources.
The time would be opportune to start a shipbuilding industry on that coast. The same thing applies to Northumberland, Gloucester, Restigouche and the whole northern coast of New Brunswick, That is a remote part of Canada, but it is a part of Canada from which communication with Europe is easy, and it might toe utilized to supply eastern Canada with a great variety of things that are very much needed. Take for instance at the present moment the question of potatoes. The people of Ottawa are paying at present 45 cents a gallon of potatoes. I remember two or three years ago at a place where I spent the summer, potatoes were selling at 50 cents a barrel.
(Mr. Loggie.)
At Montreal, potatoes are selling now at $8 a barrel; I do not know what they are selling at in Toronto, but that is a condition of affairs which should not exist. If we had these schooners able to do the business of the Baie des Chaleurs and the St. Lawrence, just as in the old days, to transport the products of the country, the cost of living would toe very materially reduced. I remember in the old days in Montreal, when I was a boy, we used to go down to the Bonsecours market and buy a peck of Malpeque oysters at 25 cents, and we could get them at $1.50 a barrel. That is an industry that has been allowed -to go almost to the vanishing point, and to-day we are paying in Montreal $15 a barrel for oysters which bear the name of Malpeque, but I do not know whether they come from there or not. That is an industry that could have been developed easily by water transportation. Is it not ridiculous to see a magnificent waterway like the St. Lawrence and all its tributaries practically unused, because while the ships that navigate the St. Lawrence are used for ocean service, or communication abroad, none of the inland trade is developed? The minister has told us that an embargo has been placed on the importation of lumber into England. This would be an opportunity to have sailing vessels and smaller craft develop our lumber industry on the Baie des Chaleurs and the St. Lawrence. We have in those districts millions of acres of timber limits which are undeveloped on account of lack of communication. In my own constituency an important syndicate some five or six years ago purchased a large timber limit, 400 square miles, for, I think, over half a million dollars. There were three or four sawmills within reach pf that limit; tout they have been closed down, and the men who were employed in them had to leave that district and go to Bathurst and other places in New Brunswick where there was communication alpng the line of the Intercolonial. This large Robitaille timber limit, one of the finest timber limits in the whole otf eastern Canada, is idle Honday for lack of communication. We have a small railway with one train a day, doing the best it can with practically no rolling stock and without locomotives able to handle the traffic. We have no sailing vessels. In the county of Gasp6 we have a syndicate from Philadelphia which has spent three or four million dollars in the last few years to establish a large pulp industry in the endeavour to develop the natural industry of that district, but there is no way by which

the products of that industry can be taken t.o Montreal. There are no bottoms by which they can be taken either to the American market or to the Canadian market, and this railway which should have been linked with the Intercolonial 25 years ago and which was intended by Sir Charles Tupper, when he received the first vote of Parliament for it, as a branch line of the Intercolonial, remains as it is to-day, and the people at Gascons say that the wharf is in such a condition that whatever sailing craft does go there is unable to stop at this wharf, and that the people have to drive twenty miles to P.ort Daniel to ship their products, as in the same cld days of long ago.
The minister should realize that a vigorous shipbuilding industry is essential and indispensable in this country. The opportunity is furnished to him now to link his name with that great industry. Were he the representative of an inland constituency, and unaware of the advantage of shipbuilding, the matter would be different. Who is not aware that no country can be truly great unless it possesses a mercantile marine? What would England be to-day without a navy; what would she have been in peace time and what would she be in war time without a navy? Why should Canada, this young giant, which is doing such great things in the railway field, and which, in other enterprises, is second to none in the world, lag behind in this matter of shipbuilding when she has half of the fresh water of the continent at her disposal?. I was amazed to hear the Minister of Marine and- Fisheries practically admit that the shipbuilders of New Brunswick had lost their cunning and that shipbuilding there was almost a lost industry. My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) corrected him on that score, and showed him that in that member's constituency the builders were prepared to go immediately into shipbuilding. The minister should take up this matter and see that it is broiight to a conclusion, because, if he does not do it himself, the time is not far distant when the public opinion of Canada will insist on the Dominion Government coming forward with a truly national shipbuilding policy for Canada.
