speechtext:
No doubt everything that can be said on behalf of shipbuilding has been said, but still I might be permitted to make a few remarks >to the minister, so far as northern New Brunswick, especially Gloucester county, is concerned. When speaking on the Budget a few days ago, I earnestly advocated shipbuilding in Canada, and particularly the building of wooden ships in the Maritime Provinces. My leaning towards the building of small wooden ships is based on the fact that while we may be building large steel ships either for 'Canada or for the Empire, and while our builders and steel manufacturers may be building steel ships after the war is over, Canada will be left altogether powerless as to her local water traffic in the future. The more steel ships we build, even if those ships are not wanted by the Imperial Government, they will, as fast as they can be built in Canada, be bought by France or other nations requiring them, and Canada will be left altogether without ships unless we -start right away to build wooden ships for our coastwise and inland service, without which our trade will be crippled in the future. Wooden ships are the only kind we shall be able to preserve for ourselves after the war is over, and every possible effort should be made to build those ships. Perhaps the minister is aware that at Bathurst, which had formerly great wooden shipbuilding yards, there is one special company to-day which would be prepared to undertake the construction of wooden ships under any favourable conditions; 500 tons has been mentioned as the limit, but ,so far as Bathurst and that company are concerned-and I name the Bathurst company, with whose general manager I have had some conversation, not recently, but some months ago-they would be willing to build ships, not only of 500 tons, but up to

1,000	tons. The impression is that in northern New Brunswick the old wooden shipbuilders have gone to their graves, but I would say for the information of the minister that born carpenters who were able, two, three or four years ago, to build wooden ships of 125, 150 or 200 tons, which have taken the highest honour among the sea-goers of the day, ought to be able to extend their genius to building ships of 500 or 1,000 tons.	,
Ships of the kind that are now being built in other parts of Canada were built at Caraquet a few years ago. Every year our fishermen build schooners of from 50 to 100 tons without any outside assistance. They cut their own lumber in the woods, and build ships which are as good a,* any that sail the seas. I think every possible effort should be made to encourage those who are in a position to build ships in northern New Brunswick. I am not asking that shipbuilding be confined to Bathurst. Every winter there is a large quantity of lumber cut on the Caraquet river, and ships of 500 tons could easily be built there, and at Tracadie. I think every effort should be made by the Government of the day and by succeeding governments to develop the shipbuilding industry in this country both now and after the war.

speechtext:
There are certain
facts with reference to the situation which are given a little more in detail in the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I see in a report that was made to the minister by Mr. Robb an account of the legislation that has been passed in other countries for the assistance of shipbuilding. There is also a statement of Great Britain's losses in merchant shipping down to March 30, 1916, which shows ' that the British steamships lost up to that date amounted to 1,320,000 tons, and sailing vessels 19,000 tons. The total Allied losses in shipping since the outbreak of war to March 30, 1916, exclusive of trawlers, of which 246 were lost, amounted to 1,658,000 tons. In view of the activity of submarines since that time, the losses down to March 31, 1917, will probably ,be double that figure, which would bring the total to over 3,000,000 tons.	.
Then there is the loss of tonnage to neutral nations, amounting to 1,977,376 tons. Of course that amount also will be very largely increased. So wh shall have a total
destruction of vessels approximating 7,000,000 tons.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext:
The latest statement I
have is that on January 1, 1917, the net loss to the British mercantile marine was a little less than five per cent of the whole.

subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext: Have you the tonnage?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext: No, only the percentage. I have the figures ,of tonnage in my office, but, unfortunately, they are not before me at the moment.

subtopic: WOODEN SAILING VESSELS UNDER CONSTRUCTION MARCH, 1917, ATLANTIC
speechtext:
I think the figures
go to indicate that mercantile vessels of not 'less than 7,000,000 in the agggregate have been removed from seas. During the year 1915 Great Britain had added 344,000 tons as her contribution towards making up that loss.
The report contains a statement of what has been done by other countries in the way of promoting construction. In Austria-Hungary, they gra^it for steamships of iron and steel $8.10 for every gross ton. In the case of sailing ships of iron and steel, when more than half of the material employed is of home production, the bounty is increased by one per cent of its amount for every one per cent of such material in excess of fifty per cent. In the case of sailing ships of wood or mixed construction, for the hull they give $2.02 for every gross ton. In Denmark they give a refund of customs duties on imported materials used for the construction of new ships. In France, in 1906, the assistance toward the construction of steamships was fixed at a maximum of $33.58 per ton, to cover both hull and machinery, and to diminish gradually for ten years. This was divided up into various amounts for hull and machinery. There was a construction bounty for sailing ships of 150 tons and over at the rate of $7.78 a ton, and for vessels of less than 150 tons at $5.84 a ton. In the German Empire the bounties do not take the form of a premium on the construction of ships, but consist, of special customs facilities for goods destined for use in shipbuilding yards, and, in the second place, of preferential railway rates. In Italy they [DOT]give bounties in the form of navigation premiums, construction and repair bounties, and remission of customs duties, during a period of fifteen years. Japan, which now comes into the world's economy on the same plane with the western nations, began shipbuilding in 1910. They provide a bounty for steel vessels of 1,000 tons or over of $5.46 to $10.93 per ton of the gross tonnage

of the hull. In Norway the assistance of bounties is to cover the amount of customs duty on imported material used in the construction of vessels. In Eussia the estimates of the Department of Mercantile Marine included, for 1909 and subsequent years, a sum of $51,428.52 for the encouragement of shipbuilding.
An interesting statement is given of the tonnage of Canadian vessels from 1874 to 1916. This shows the transition of our registration. Comparing 1874 with 1915, the figures show as follows:-
	1874.	1915.
Province.	Tons.	Tons.New Brunswick	. 294,741	56,219Nova Scotia	. 479,669	125,567Quebec	. 218,946	267,897Ontario	. 113,008	312,971P. E. Island	. 48,338	11,518British Columbia	. 3,611	144,835It is rather surprising	to observe	by the
figures showing where registration of vessels takes place. In Collingwood, Ont., which is a construction point, the registration in 1915 was only 15,500 tons. In Toronto the registration amounted to 64,000 tons. A large registration is found at Port Arthur and also at Ottawa, these, I suppose, being small vessels for use on the lakes.
There has been construction of steel vessels in Montreal, and also in certain Ontario ports for some time. Steel vessels are now constructed in British Columbia. Their supply of plates must be drawn from points in the United States. I see no reason why British Columbia should present special advantages for the building of steel ships over other portions of the Dominion, as there is no supply of steel plates there. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has told us that steel plates for the construction of ships are not to be had in Canada. I know that they are not manufactured here, but I think it is imperative that the Government should assist the construction of steel vessels in Canada by taking up this question of the production of steel plates. The Government are not going to be in any better shape to launch a shipbuilding policy after the war if they do not, in the meantime, provide for the production of steel plates in Canada.	.
Everything that can be made in steel, with the exception of large structural steel, which is now only made in Pittsburg, is made by the various steel industries of this country, and the question of encouraging the construction of steel plates in our steel industry, which has reached colossal proportions, is one that the Government should direct their attention to now. It is no use

talking of building vessels after the war if the Government is not going to move in the meantime in reference to assisting to develop the proposition of making steel plates in our steel industries. I am at a loss to know what the minister meant when he spoke about the Government assisting the steel industry in connection with the shipbuilding industry if the assistance that is required is not to be given until after the war. If they mean to do - anything after the war in regard to steel shipbuilding, they will be about as far ahead in the matter as they are to-day unless they begin now to assist in the manufacture of steel plates.
With regard to the construction of wooden vessels, it is all nonsense for the minister to say that the Government want to do what the British Government are doing through the Imperial Munitions Board in connection with the construction of wooden ships of a certain class. If the Government want to do anything similar in order to get a merchant marine, they can start by building .smaller vessels, for which they can get numerous contracts placed all over the Maritime Provinces. The minister does not answer this problem by reading a statement of the number of vessels that are being built, and telling us what the British Government are doing through the Imperial Munitions Board. The minister told us that the thing that was nearest to his heart was to have a Canadian mercantile marine. He is perfectly willing that Great Britain should build these ships through the Imperial Munitions Board, but he is not willing that the Canadian Government should do anything for their own shipbuilding industry. Why wait until after the war? Why, in view of the story of the wholesale destruction and disappearance from the sea of such a tremendous quantity of tonnage as
7,000,000 tons, should we in Canada not do anything to build either wooden or steel . ships until after the war? What was the meaning of Mr. Lloyd George's appeal: Give us ships and more ships to win the war? Is Canada not going to do anything in regard to that matter? Are we simply going to guarantee the credit of Great Britain to the extent of $10,000,000 and say that our duty has been fulfilled, and all the aid that we can give in this matter has been given? When the minister said that no ships would have been built in Canada but for that credit, he made a statement that I listened to with amazement. Are we to be told that Great

Britain had placed in the United States contracts for over a thousand vessels and that she preferred to go to the United States rather than to come to Canada? If so, it is time we found it out. When we are told the British Government would not come to Canada to build ships unless the Canadian Government agreed to provide a credit for them, I want to know why they went to the United States to build ships. They went without getting a credit from the Government of the United States. The reason they went there was purely a business proposition. Why should they not have come to Canada? Unless there is a move made by the Government we are in this unfortunate position that we will have no mercantile marine at all between what has been destroyed and what has been commandeered by the British Government. It will be almost impossible to handle our natural products on the sea or to carry on our interprovincial trade and the result will be that when the war is over, if we are going to do nothing, we * will have no mercantile marine to build up our trade and the whole thing will be gone. We will have no provision in this country for the manufacture of steel plate which will enable us to undertake steel shipbuilding and under these circumstances the imperative demand is that the Government should move now and do something.

[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My recollection is that the agent at Pdctou was receiving $1,000 a year. His duties were largely in connection with the crossing to Prince Edward Island and the management of the boats during the winter months. In view of the changes which were made in that service, and acting on what I thought was the absolutely correct information given by my officials, I decided that the office should be closed. I did not think that the work done would be sufficient to justify the continuance of an agency there. Reports were subsequently made to me, however, by officials of the department, pointing out that this agent had been doing other work as well in connection with the Department of Naval Service, the remuneration for which was covered by his salary as agent for the Marine and Fisheries Department.
In consequence of those reports which I received from the Inspector of the Marine Agencies and other officials in my department, I decided to continue the office, but at a salary of only $400, which it occurred to me would be sufficient to cover the work which the agent would do. The policy of the department would be to continue the agency there but at the reduced salary of $400 instead of $1,000.

Is the minister
aware of the necessity of telephonic communication with Pictou Island? I understand that it was brought to his attention. There is an absolute necessity of having telephonic communication with the island if the life-saving station is to be made of any practical value. The life-saving station is-at a point about ten miles away from the nearest telegraph or telephone, and there is no way of communicating in the event of a wreck. A cable was to be laid,
I think, in conjunction with the Government; I understand that petitions have been sent to the department asking for that, and I am instructed that Mr. Nickerson, the late inspector of life-saving stations, recommended to the department the necessity of furnishing some means of communication with the island.

I asked the minister for information in regard to appointments in his department under section 21 of the Civil Service Act. Perhaps I had better read the section in order that he may fully understand what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand it.

Section 21 of the Civil Service Act reads:
If the deputy head reports that the knowledge and ahility requisite for the position are wholly or in part professional, technical or otherwise peculiar, the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the head1 of the department based on the report in writing of the deputy head, may appoint a person to the position without competitive examination and without reference to the age limit, provided the said person obtains from the Commission a certificate, to be given with or without examination, as is determined by the regulations of the Commission, that he possesses the requisite knowledge and ahility and is duly qualified as to health, character and habits.
I discovered that a very large number of appointments were being made by the present Administration under section 21, and I was trying to ascertain from the various departments why they found it necessary to resort so generally to this section. There are not a very large number in the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Six, I think.

I find from a return
that there were two appointments after competitive examination and four without competitive examination in the Marine and Fisheries Department. In the Naval Service, there were four appointed after competitive examination and two without competitive examination, making twelve altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Ten altogether, is it not?

No, twelve. The purpose of the Civil Service Act was that civil servants should be appointed wholly on their merits after competitive examination, and it is important for the efficiency of the service that this rule be strictly adhered to. I understand that occasionally a friend of the Government desires to obtain an appointment in some department, and he is perhaps too old to ibe taken in under the ordinary rules, or unable to pass an examination, and in that event section 21 is resorted to. This was never intended at the time the Act was passed. This section was intended for the appointment of officials with professional or technical ability. The explanation given when the Act was passed in 1908 was that occasionally the Government would require to introduce into the Civil Service some eminent man from abroad or perhaps from Canada who would not be willing to submit himself to an examination by the commission, or who, perhaps, would be over age. The Marine Department might want an engineer or some man of ability, and if such a one were appointed no one would complain; but when we find that the present Administration has appointed 174 men under section 21, it is clear to every one that there is an abuse. We want to ascertain who is the sinner who is perpetrating these abuses, and while I do not say that the Minister of Marine has perpetrated any, I would like to have from him the information as to whom he has appointed in his department, the name of each, age at the time of appointment, former employment, present employment, salary paid, and the reason why section 21 was resorted to in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In the Department of Marine and Fisheries, during the period of nearly six years that I have been head of that department, there have been six such appointments, as is shown by a return laid on the table of the House. I do not know whether I can name the officials from memory, but I can name some. One is Mr. 
Ge'orge Herbert Flood, who was appointed purchasing agent of the department. When I came into office, the purchasing agent was Mr. Cecil Doutre, who was a very satisfactory official. Mr. Doutre felt that he could earn a larger salary and improve his position outside of the department, and, very much to my regret, he resigned. The position of purchasing agent is one of great importance. After discussing the matter with my officials, I came to the conclusion that it was absolutely necessary to have in that position some one who had previous experience, not only in business, but in the business of the department itself. It occurred to us it would be proper to promote one of the agents, and, on looking over the list of agents, we concluded that the best appointment we could make would be that of Mr. George Herbert Flood, who was agent of the department in the city of St. John, and who had been appointed a few years before I came into office. Speaking offhand, I may say that at the time of his appointment he was a man of about forty-five or forty-six years, perhaps a little more. His record in the department was wonderfully good; we regarded him as a competent official, and we decided in the interest of the department that we could not do better than to appoint Mr. Flood. In consequence	of	his age, we	hadto appoint	him under section	21.
If I recollect aright, the Civil Service Commissioners approved of his qualifications. Another gentleman appointed under this section was Mr. McDonell, in connection with the shipping branch of the department. He had been in the department for five years when this vacancy occurred. An examination was held, which he passed most satisfactorily, and which showed that he possessed the necessary technical knowledge. His position is assistant to the chairman of the Board of Steamship Inspection, which requires considerable technical knowledge and skill regarding the construction of ships, boilers, and so forth. Another gentleman appointed under this section was Mr. Thomas Ferguson, the present chairman of the Board of Steamship Inspection. He had been in the outside service for a good many years, and was considered to be the best qualified man for this position.
Perhaps the minister could give me all the names and particulars later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be glad to do so when the Naval estimates are before the House.

I see toy a return brought down a few days ago that there has been practically no increase in the staff of the Department of Marine and Fisheries during the last four or five years, tout that there has been a large increase in the expenditure of the department.

I am speaking of the Fisheries Department.

speechtext: Yes, but the Fisheries are administered by the Department of Naval Service. My hon. friend will recollect that we have discussed this time and again in the House. About three years ago, in order to equalize the work of the two departments, one of which was heavy and the other comparatively light, the Fisheries were brought under the Department of the Naval Service.
The increase is therefore in the staff of the Naval Department.

increase in the staff of the Marine and Fisheries Department.

but I shall be glad to give my hon. friend the information when the Naval Estimates are up.	.

I should like to draw the minister's attention to the lighting of the Rideau canal. I was under the impression that that was done by the Department of Railways and Canals. I brought to the attention of the Minister of Railways a few days ago the fact that the canal had been lighted above. Smith's Falls, that is, that portion running through Leeds, Lanark, Grenville and Frontenac counties, but that portion running through the counties of Russell and Carleton had not been lighted this season. Possibly this is an omission, which will be rectified on the minister's attention being directed to it. I do not wish to delay the committee at all, and I will take the liberty of sending my hon. friend a small file of correspondence tomorrow, knowing that he will have the matter attended to. It is represented to me that there are about 1,000 power boats on this waterway, representing an investment of at least $1,000,000, and that by reason of the increased production taking place along the canal and the river there will be a great increase in navigation this year. The prospect is also held out that unless present conditions materially change, coal may be brought down this waterway as in years past. For these reasons, the lighting of what is represented to me to be possibly the most dangerous part of the channel is a very important matter, and if my hon. friend will be good enough to say he will have this matter attended to, I will send him the correspondence tomorrow or the next day.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be very glad to attend to the matter. The procedure when lights are applied for is to send the applications to the Lighthouse Board of Canada, which consists of the deputy minister and the chief engineer of the department, the inspector of lights, and the Chairman of the Shipping Federation of Canada, and the Chairman of the Dominion Marine Association. The board meets regularly, and when an application comes before them for a light or a buoy or some other aid to navigation, the matter is referred to them and they get reports from the inspector of lights and other sources, and then decide whether the request shall be granted. There is also a gentleman on the Pacific coast, Captain Troup, who deals with these matters on that side of the continent.

That would be the procedure in case a new light or buoy was

asked for, but in this case the lights have been in existence, but they have not been placed this season.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will look into that.
Maintenance and repairs to lighthouses, $750,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is to provide for the maintenance of aids to navigation, including the cost of supplies, such as fuel, illum-inants, cleaning material and other supplies, with the delivery of the same, and also the cost of repairs to these aids to - navigation. The amount spent in this service in 1915-16 was $604,000, and last year it was $654,000. The increase was mainly due to the higher prices of supplies. The expenditure was divided by provinces as follows. Nova Scotia, $125,000; Prince Edward Island, $13,000; New Brunswick, $94,000; Quebec $123,000; Montreal, $51,000; Ontario, $94,000; British Columbia, $77,000; General, $14,700. The cost of this work of maintenance cannot be predetermined, but the officer whose business it is to report on this matter says that the amount asked for will be ample for the year. We will keep the expenditure as low as possible, though it is difficult to . keep it down on account of the increased cost of supplies.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Is anything being done with regard to Ingonish harbour, in Victoria county? It was deepened twelve years ago, but before that it was rather a bar harbour. The entrance to the harbour is under the famous Cape Smoky, the highest peak in Nova Scotia, and I understand that the engineer sent report on the project, advised that range lights could not be placed there on account of the height and steepness of the mountain. There are aids to navigation there which are fairly useful in the daytime, but which do not help at night. This harbour is very much used, especially for fishermen and large vessels for shelter, and also by three or four steamers running between Halifax and Cape Breton and Newfoundland. I have advised putting lighted buoys at the entrance of this harbour. Three or four on either side would be much help.

speechtext: While there is use for a lighthouse at Triple Island at the entrance to Prince Rupert harbour, and while it is work that will have to be undertaken in the near future, it may not be necessary to proceed with it this year. These are the principal items of work that will be undertaken this year.
Does it include aids to navigation in Hudson Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are not contemplating any additional expenditures in Hudson Bay this year.
Have you already some lighthouses in Hudson Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, buoys, lighthouses and beacons. If conditions were normal we would do more, but there is very great difficulty in getting ships to carry stuff or to work there.

Are there any lights in
operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are either in operation or they are ready to be put in operation the moment the necessity arises.
What has the minister done in the way of lighting Hudson Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Down through the straits there have been placed ten or twelve lights -I think ten lights-and beacons.
Is there any light or beacon on Mansfield Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Is the wireless station there under my hon. friend's department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is under the department of the Naval Service.
What amount was spent last year in Hudson Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My deputy will look it up in the Auditor General's report.

Would the minister explain what it is proposed to do at Anticosti Island? I visited Anticosti some years ago and met Mr. Menier's representative, and he told me that they had negotiated with the department to take over some lights which Mr. Menier had erected. I understand it is proposed to render the north channel navigable.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. The negotiations with Mr. Menier took place before I was in the department, but I have heard the matter discussed in the department and I understand the department took oveT all the lights on the island with the exception of one which they decided not to take over because they thought that Mr. Menier had erected that simply for his own personal benefit, and it was not in general use as an aid to navigation. The lights for which provision is being made on the north side of the island are to be erected so that ships can pass through the northern channel with safety. This is done at the suggestion of the authorities of the Admiralty, who believe that under existing conditions and because of the submarine danger, it may be necessary to use that north channel to an extent and in a way that it was never used before, and these lights are being established there as a guide to mariners.
Are there any lights indicating Churchill harbour on Hudson Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

I suppose there are at
Nelson harbour?

Have they floated away?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, they have 'been looked after and taken, care of. They are taken up in the fall and put down again when navigation opens.

Is it the policy of the
department to stop expenditure in Hudson Bay for the present or'until after the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a matter that has not been decided. We will be guided by circumstances. With the great scarcity of vessels which was spoken of this afternoon it is very doubtful whether many vessels will go into Hudson Bay this year. But we have the straits fairly well lighted now. That is an enormous improvement and adds very much to the safety of navigation. We are prepared to do what is necessary if it is in the public interest that it should be done.

Lighthouse and Coast Service-Signal service, $60,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This service has been in
existence for a good many years and was established to maintain communication between ship and shore by .means of flag signals. It extends from St. John and Halifax to Cape Race and Belle Isle, and up the gulf and river St. Lawrence and the lakes as far as Sault Ste. Marie. The agents at the different points receive small salaries, some of them $200 and some more. These stations report the movements of vessels to Montreal, Quebec, Sydney, Halifax and St. John. They report water conditions daily to Montreal, Quebec, Halifax or St. John. Montreal, Quebec and St. John publish daily bulletins giving ice and weather

conditions, and movements of vessels. Montreal publishes daily the depth of water in the various parts of the ship channel. The signal service offices at Montreal, Quebec and St. John are open day and night to furnish to the public information regarding shipping matters. The telegraph system of the Department of Public Works on the north shore of the St. Lawrence reports the movements of vessels engaged in the coasting trade, to the signal service at Quebec. The collectors of customs on the St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic coast and the bay of Fundy report the arrival and departure of vessels engaged in overseas traffic to Lloyd's agent at Quebec or St. John.
How does the information of the movement of vessels reach the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Before the war all of that information was published in the newspapers. Publication has ceased since the beginning of the war.

Has my hon. friend considered the importance to owners of getting this information about their vessels? The owner of a vessel whose head office is in Montreal may have a ship which passes Cape Race on the way to England, or inward bound. It would be very important for him to know that the ship had passed Cape Race at a given hour. The information might reach the Marine Department hut not the owner if he did not happen to live in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The agent or owner of the vessel is communicated with by the shipping office; that information is furnished to him by the signal officer at Montreal or whatever port it may he.
I suppose it would be an advantage to have the signal officer at Cape Race wire at once to the owner.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The way it practically works out is that the man, say at Cape Race, wires to the port to which he reports the names of all vessels that have passed inward or outward. He does that twice a day.

I know, as a matter of fact, that the agents at the stations the minister has mentioned do not report to owners of vessels when they pass
9	p.m. these points; at least I know of cases* where they have not done so. I also know of cases where the owners

have made private arrangements with the signal officers to get the information when tire vessels pass. This is a very important and useful service, and its administration might be greatly improved if the minister would investigate it and see that regulations are made that would give this information to the owners of the vessels, and, in ordinary times, to the public.
Lighthouse and Coast Service-Administration of pilotage and maintenance and repairs to steamer Eureka, $56,300.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is the expenditure in connection with pilotage on the St. Lawrence and the maintenance of the Eureka, which is kept at Father Point where pilots board and leave vessels. During a portion of the time they live on the steamboat. The vote is the same as last year, and we spent last year about $42,000.
Is the whole of this expended in the St. Lawrence?
