speechtext: Yes.
Are the pilots still taken on and off at Father Point?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Was any effect given to the recommendations, made some time ago after the loss of a steamer there, with regard to the taking on and off of pilots?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Every recommendation
made by the Pilotage Commission which was appointed some years ago was carried out, with the exception of that with regard to the pilots. In order to carry out that recommendation we have to have two boats instead of one, but so far we have not provided an additional boat.
Maintenance and repairs to wharves, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: After wharves have been constructed by the Public Works Department they automatically come under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries so far as ordinary management and the collection of revenue are concerned. The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, then appoints a wharfinger, whose business it is to collect the tolls and look after the wharves. Repairs amounting to $50 or over are attended to by the Department of Public Works; those under $50 are made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. This sum of $10,000 is for that purpose. Last year we expended only $5,460 and in 1915-16 about $8,000.
Whose duty is it to look after the repairs to these wharves in the province of Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the wharf is out of repair, it is the duty of the wharfinger to report to the department. If the repairs required are of an extensive character, his report is forwarded to the Public Works officer in the province who is instructed to report to the Chief Engineer at Ottawa. This is a very old system. I rather think that the Department of Marine and Fisheries should have larger control of expenditures in connection with repairs, as it otherwise has complete control of the wharves.
How are the wharfingers paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Like the harbour masters
they are allowed a certain percentage of the collections up to a certain amount. In [DOT] some cases the collections are a negative quantity because some of the wharves used by the fishermen are exempt from tolls.
Is it the custom of the department to appoint a wharfinger when a wharf is handed over tp it >by the. Public Works Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the custom, but the remuneration is so small that in some cases it is impossible to get a man in the neighbourhood who will act as wharfinger.

Last year a
small expenditure was made at Margaree Harbour upon a pier which was constructed primarily for the purpose of directing the current of the Margaree river. Shortly afterward, the fishermen commenced to use the pier for the landing of their fish. The department subsequently appointed a wharfinger who proceeded to collect tolls from the fishermen-the first time that had been done in the history of the place. It is absurd that a wharfinger should be employed on that pier, and I would suggest that the minister cancel the appointment forthwith.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will look info the matter.

What is the gross
amount received by way of revenue from the wharves?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In 1915-16, $56,261, an increase of $23,037 over the previous year. $36,908 of that amount was collected in New Brunswick, of which $34,000 was collected at the city of St. John from the large wharves that were built by the Public Works Department a short time ago.

How much of that
money was used in paying the wharfingers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think this was the net
amount received.
What percentage was paid in St. John to the wharfingers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are three wharves at St. John. When I came into office there was one wharf, of which Mr. Elkin is the wharfinger. He receives $1,500 a year. When the second wharf was finished, Mr Cowan, who, I am sorry to say, died the other day, was appointed wharfinger, and he received a similar salary. When the third wharf was completed, I did not appoint a wharfinger; I made an arrangement by which the work would be done through the office of the Department of Marine and Fisheries in the city of St. John. I thought that was a better arrangement. As a matter of fact, we are at present considering the advisability of doing away altogether with these wharfingers and placing the responsibility of collecting the rents in the hands of the agent of the Marine and Fisheries Department. I have not yet come to a conclusion, but I have ask^d my officials for a report as to the advisability of taking that course.
I feel I should appeal to my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to have repairs done at. Perce wharf in the county of Gaspe.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Would the repairs cost more than $50?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend
should make his appeal to the Minister cf Public Works.

-As that minister is not in the House and as he is not very often in the House, I appeal to a gentleman who honours us with his presence. The whart having been completed, has been transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and therefore, diplomatically speaking, the recommendation for the repairs should come through the Marine Department. This wharf was built some years ago when I had the honour to represent the county of Gaspe. Perce is the shire town for the whole district, and there is quite a steamer service between Quebec, Montreal, and the Bale des Chaleurs, as well as between Oampbellton and Dalhousie. The Perce wharf is the most important in that district, and I am sure it pays its way, but during the last three or four years it has been completely abandoned; no repairs

have been made to it, and, as a result-and I saw the wharf last summer-it has been cut in two by the seas. It is a great pity that a wharf which has cost in the neighbourhood of fifty or sixty thousand dollars should become a ruin owing to the indifference of the Department of Public Works. I would advise my hon. friend to represent to the Minister of Public Works that this wharf should be properly repaired, because the public are nrow obliged to travel in badges a mile or two out from the harbour to get on board the steamer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall be glad to make
representations to the Minister of Public Works.

I should like t.o make a
similar request on behalf of the wharf at Gascons which is not veTy far distant from Perce. This wharf has broken in two and it has been utterly abandoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There i- a question on the Order Paper about it

Yes. Gascons is an important point. The people there have to go about twenty miles to Port Daniel where there is another wharf, and that is a great inconvenience. The same remark applies to the wharf at St. Charles de Caplan and the wharf at Bonaventure. General repairs to those wharves are required. The policy, during the war, to put the case mildly, seems to have been not to spend anything in that district, and very little has been done, the result being that Government property is becoming dilapidated. I should like to ask the minister about the wharf at Miguasha Point off Dalhousie which was built by the Department of Public Works and which after remaining under the control of that department for some time, was transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. After the appointment of a wharfinger, an attempt was made to collect tolls. The wharf is used largely by market gardeners who go to Dalhousie and who are unwilling to pay the-tolls, and I understand that the ferry boat refuses to land at the wharf. Has the department abandoned the collection of tolls, or will it insist on collecting them during the present season.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My experience in regard to these small wharves is that the Government gets such a very small revenue out of them and it is so objectionable to the people to pay these tolls that the country would not be any worse off if we abolished the tolls altogether. You need a responsible man

in charge of each wharf to see that it is properly conducted, and it seems reasonable that the country should pay a man for that purpose. I know that there is nothing that country people taking produce to market hate so much as to have to pay a small toll on their produce going over a wharf. I will make inquiries in regard to the wharf at Miguasha Point.
'Mr. MABCT'L:	What arrangement is
being made with regard to the collection of tolls at Baie des Chaleurs wharves Formerly the wharfingers were paid fifty per cent of the tolls collected, or, in round figures, about $50 a year. I understand that a few years ago- an arrangement was made that the boat proprietor paid a round sum to the department and 'received permission to use free of charge all the wharves on the coast. What arrangements are to be made for the present season? We expect to have a boat this year which comes from St. John. The boat we had last year was very unsatisfactory, it was a very small river boat. The Minister of Trade and Commerce explained to me that he could not find anything better. It is a pure waste of money to put a boat p.f that kind on the Baie des Chaleurs; there are no cabins on it, and a passenger who wishes to take the whole trip, must have a cabin. Owing to lack of cabins, this boat goes only half the distance and returns. Last year it started its services on the 5th of August, and the whole 'season it carried only 150 passengers and about 200 tons of freight.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Even if there were a good boat on that service, is it not a fact that a great many people would travel >by train? There is a train service each way each day, and I think the tendency of the people 

I have been down there sometimes-is to patronize the railway because the trains run both winter and summer. Even a good boat would find difficulty in attracting enough patronage to make it a paying proposition. 1 will look into the matter of an arrangement for using the wharf. I know there !ha,s been [such an arrangement as my hon. friend refers to.
How many wharves are there under the department in Chatham, and what was the revenue last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have a list here of the wharves that have paid revenue, but there is no mention of a wharf at Chatham.

There is one wharf there under the department. There are three public wharves, but two of them are under
the jurisdiction of the Railway Department. The other wharf, which is under my hon. friend's department, is in the rear of the Customs House and post office, and the storm signals and buoys are located on it each winter. I see no reason why there should not be some revenue from that wharf.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the wharf was used simply for putting up buoys and chains and that sort of thing, there would be no revenue from it.
It is used for general purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I never heard of it before, and I am glad my hon. friend has drawn my attention to the matter. I will have it looked into.

There are quite a number of wharves in the county of Victoria, and some of them at least are paying wharfage. There is a wharf at Baddeck, and another at Ferry Landing or Little Narrows, as it is sometimes called.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The wharf at Baddock pays something.
Are there any wharves at South Bay, North Bay and White Point?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Baddeck is the only one that is mentioned here, but if my hon. friend would send me a list I could get him the information.

Most of these wharves are in fishing villages. I understand that some local men tried to collect wharfage and tolls from the fishermen, and it caused a great deal of trouble. I think I heard the minister say this evening that where wharves are used for the accommodation of fishermen no tolls are charged. I would suggest to the minister that instead of appointing a wharfinger to look after these- wharves, it would be better to leave it to some one who is in business near the wharf and has occasion to use it practically every day. Wharfingers have very often no occasion to go to the wharf unless something comes for them by boat, but there is always some one in business near these wharves. I have particularly in mind a place called Washabuck, where there has been a wharf for about twelve yeaTS. A gentleman named McNeil is in business at the head of the wharf and has occasion to use it practically every day. He takes as much pride in it as if it were his own, and certainly keeps it in good

shape. I 'do not know whether anything is collected from this wharf, hut it is certainly a first class one. I am sure that in all the villages along the coast the minister *will find men of this sort who will take much better care of the wharf than -wharfingers, who have no interest in the -wharf except collecting a little toll and receiving any goods that come for themselves. These wharves were built in the county of Victoria for the accommodation of the different villages along the coast, and with no intention of collecting wharfage or tolls of any kind. A fishing wharf serves two purposes as a rule: it acts as a breakwater and shelter for the fishing boats, and serves also the general purposes of a wharf. They were put up to assist the fishermen. If the minister finds that tolls are being collected at any of these wharves, at White Point or any other place in the county of Victoria, I would suggest that he cut it out at once, because it is a great nuisance to the fishermen, and the revenue is of no consequence to the department. There is a good deal of dissatisfaction at Baddeck by reason of the collection of wharfage. There should not be a wharfage charge there at all. Eight across the water from Baddeck there is a wharf at Iona, which I suppose is under the control of my hon. friend's department, and which is used in connection with the Intercolonial. The Kailway Department has laid rails down to the wharf, and cars from the Intercolonial are shunted down, and the freight for Victoria county is carried by the Government railway to this wharf. The goods are put upon a fairly large ferry boat running between Iona and Baddeck. The Government, having taken the freight from the wharf, must land it somewhere, 'and I .submit that the same rule should apply at Baddeck as applies at Iona. Although the railway is not in my hon. friend's department, it is all under the one Government.
If the man at Iona does not pay wharfage when getting goods over the Intercolonial, why should the man. at Baddeck be called upon to pay? When I had more to do with the management of these affairs, there were no toll charges, there. The people got their goods off the train, and carried them away. We built a first-class warehouse there to shelter goods, and .there was a man there willing to look after it because of some little advantages he got in landing his own goods and in the use of the warehouse. The system that was. in use then should be resumed. The amount to be collected under

the present plan is small, but it is annoying. The thing should be abandoned.

In corroboration of what my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has said, I may remind the minister that in the session of 1908 or 1909 the present Mr. Justice Brodeur, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, made the declaration that tolls should not be collected from the fishermen for the use of the wharves along our coasts. Of course, if a fisherman used his boat for business purposes for pant of the season, toll would be collected. That has been the practice in Gloucester county, as -the Minister of Marine knows very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Fishermen are not charged when using these wharves in connection with their work as fishermen.
What does the minister say with regard to Baddeck wharf?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The law provides that in
th$se cases a wharfinger must be appointed and fees collected, and until the law is changed I should not be justified in saying that tolls shall not be collected at Baddeck any more than in saying that they should not be collected at St. John., at which point they amount to over $33,000 a year. I. notice that Baddeck pays something over $200, and is the third largest wharf in Nova Scotia, <the largest being Digby, which, I think, pays about $1,700, and the second-largest Kingsport, about $600.
I agree that these wharves were built in most cases simply for the benefit of the people who had access to them, but I think Parliament thought it only fair thg,t those who used the wharves should pay something toward keeping them in repair. Of course, in some cases, the amount collected is trifling, so trifling as to be hardly worth the trouble of collection. But if the principle laid down by the hon. gentleman is to be carried into effect, the question of where the line is to be drawn would have to be carefully considered, in order that the country might not be imp.osed upon and its proper revenues left uncollected.

I agree that where a
Government wharf is in competition with other wharves, or in the case of any Government wharf in a large commercial centre, such as St. John, Halifax or Digby. *wharfage should be collected. But when goods come over the Government railway to Baddeck, freight is paid on them to that point. The Government ha? a wharf in connection with the rpad at Baddeck, just as

it has a wharf in connection with the road at Iona. The Government must have a place to deliver goods, and for Baddeok the wharf is the place where they are delivered. It is a part of the system which must be used by the railway in delivering its freight

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
But would npt this be a
similar case: A Montreal merchant makes a contract for goods in Liverpool, to be delivered on the wharf at Montreal. Should the people from whom the goods are bought pay the wharfage charges, or would the hon. gentleman say that no wharfage charge should be made by the owners of the wharf, the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal?

But if the Government railway undertook to carry the goods from Montreal to Baddeck and to deliver them at Baddeck, they, having a wharf of their own there, should not charge wharfage to the owner of the goods. In the case to which the hon. minister refers, if the steamship company whose vessel carries the goods from Liverpool to Montreal have a wharf of their own in connection with their steamship line, then, having charged a freight rate to cover everything, they should not charge wharfage for delivery on their own wharf.
The one charge is supposed to cover everything because when tb,e goods are delivered on the wharf at Iona, there is no wharfage at all, but it is a wharf just as much as it is a wharf at Baddeck. The Railway Department recognize the fact and include the charge for wharfage there because it is necessary to the delivery of goods that they shall pass over the wharf.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It all depends on the contract they make with the people as to what they shall charge.

I am only talking about a matter of -fair dealing as between the Intercolonial railway and a citizen. That is perhaps the only case of the kind along the Intercolonial. I do not know of any other case where they take goods which have to go over the water before they are delivered. Where there is a Government wharf at which goods are delivered I always contended when the late Liberal Government was in power-and I almost succeeded in convincing the minister-they should not charge because it is part of their own system.
To provide for breaking- ice in Thunder Bay and Lake Superior and other points deemed advisable for the good of navigation, $40,000.
How many icebreakers have you in Thunder Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have no icebreakers of our own in Thunder Bay. We have to make a contract to have the work done.
How much was spent last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Our contract is for $30,000.
It is with the Canadian Towing and Wrecking Company with which Mr. Whelan is connected. I am not quite sure what we spent but $30,000 is the amount we have to pay every year.
Does the contract go on from year to year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The contract is for three years from December, 1914, and expires in December of this year.
Will it be thrown open to the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we always put it up to competition and give it to the lowest tenderer.
How could you get tenders for icebreaking when some years you have no ice at all. Some years you have lots of ice and other years you have thin ice.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Sometimes we have very thin ice. We have to take our chances.
Repairs to maritime road, $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That item was passed the other night.
This is a road to a lighthouse?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is a maritime road leading to a lighthouse in an out-of-the-way place. There is a long stretch of road with nobody living on it, it carries the Government telephone line and it is for the purpose of keeping it in repair that this' $1,000 is given.
Might I mention a road in my county that is in a very bad condition. It is the road between the lighthouse and the village of Escuminac, some four or five miles in length.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is there anyone living on the road?

No. During most of the season there is no person at Escuminac Point except the light-keeper. During the summer there are two fishermen and -there are two lobster factories operated there. The road is practically impassable.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I suppose the lobster fishermen go there by boats?
They do in some cases, but they would like also to use this road which is practically impassable.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Could you get over it in an automobile?

You might, but there
would be danger of getting stuck on the road. Some money was spent on this road by the department five or six years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That seems to establish a precedent.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will have the matter
looked into. If the road is necessary for the lighthouse, and not necessary for other purposes, it is only fair that we should help to maintain it. But, if the road is used by the people who are interested in running the 'lobster canneries and the fishermen I do not say it would be unfair that the department should make some grant towards it but it would be only fair that they should at least contribute towards the expense as well.
I think that was done before.
If this road was built for the lighthouse it would be the duty of the minister to keep it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I fancy you will find that the road was there before the lighthouse was built.

I have a similar case at Pointe Maquereaux. The municipal council of Gascon applied for a grant to put in order the road leading to the lighthouse. The department sent an inspector down, he reported against the application and the department refused to make any grant. The last news I had was that the road was practically impassible. The road leads from the main Gaspe road to the Pointe Mac-quereaux light. A small grant of $200 or $300 would put the road in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will make a note of it.
Amount required to pay pension of $300 each per annum to retired pilots. $8,700.
Are these the same pensioners that we had last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, with the exception that two have died since last year, Charles Brown and Pierre Pipon. The arrange-

ment under which this amount is paid is familiar to members of the late Administration as it was made during their tenure of office. It became necessary to decrease the number of pilots in the Quebec district and it was agreed to give these men, during their lifetime, $300 a year. Under that agreement it is necessary to vote this amount.
Will the minister explain how it is that if two have died there are still the same number as last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There must' be two less.
I find that there are 29 in the Auditor General's Report for last year and 29 in this list.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How do you account for that?.
I suppose two others came on.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But we are asking for $600 less.
The amounts paid are not always the same because according to the Auditor General's Report some get $300 and some less than $300.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understood $300. I gave the explanation that two had died and I understood that that explained the difference. .
My hon. friend explained last year that when these pilots died we would get rid of this expenditure but I find two names on the list this year that were not on last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think that some of the names were omitted from the main estimates last year, and were inserted in the supplementary estimates. That would account for the difference.

My hon. friend can see that it is difficult for us coming from other parts of Maritime Canada to defend pensions given to pilots on the St. Lawrence when they are not given to pilots in other places who are just as deserving. I am not complaining about the payment of pensions to pilots on the St. Lawrence if they are entitled to them, hut I have in my mind men on the coast of Nova Scotia, in my county, at places like Canso, Isaac's Harbour and the St. Mary river, who have for many years done the pilotage work of that stormy coast, who have grown old in the service, who have always been faithful, and, so far as I can see, are as well entitled

to some retiring allowance as those on the St. Lawrence river. If there is an agree' ment by which we are liable to pay these pensions to these pilots, of course we must carry it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the unfortunate part of it.
But if my hon. friend is going to add to the number year by year I must come in with certain pilots in whom 1 am interested, and ask to have them put on the list too. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have some of my own. I think the criticism of my hon. friend is perfectly fair. It seems strange and incongruous, but this is not my infant at all; I have inherited this item as any future Minister of Marine and Fisheries will have to do, and I have no doubt that when the arrangement was made it commended itself to those in charge of the Marine Department as a fair and proper arrangement. They were familiar with the facts; an agreement' was made, and there is nothing for us to do but to act in good faith. We cannot repudiate an agreement made honestly with the pilots by the Government.
What worries me is the two men who rose uip and took the places of the two dead men.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: That covers the item I spoke of earlier in regard to telephones?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I do not think it does.

In this case it does, because the lighthouse and the life-saving station are alongside of each other. If there ever was a case where a lighthouse required to be connected by telephone it is this case. There are two lighthouses on this island. A cable passes close to the island, and the question is if it could not be utilized to give telephone communication to those two islands. In winter the lane of communication between the mainland and Prince Edward Island passes by these islands, the steamers go past there all the time. An ice shove or anything of that kind might occur and a steamer might be ashore there for hours and be destroyed by the ice without there being any means of
communicating with the mainlaifd and obtaining assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There have been reports upon this, but all the papers are in the other department whose Estimates will be taken up later on. There seems to be little necessity for this item in my Estimates. For years a small amount has been voted each year to enable the more important light stations to be brought into telephone communication with the nearest settlement where this appears to be desirable in the public interest. The telephone enables meteorological and other observations to be * sent in promptly, and is of great use in case of shipwreck. The expenditure under this head in 1915-16 was $1.50, and last year it was nothing, so I do not see that there can be any very pressing need for these telephone lines. If I do not find any need for it this year, I will not bring the item in again. I think it would take much more than $500 to carry out the suggestion of my hon. friend in reference to Pictou island.
Would the minister say whether it is proposed to spend any money for the protection of the harbour lights in Pictou?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The matter has not been brought to my attention.
I understand that some survey or observation was made last autumn.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not hesitate to say that if any expenditure is necessary in order to maintain the light, it will be made; but no report has been made to me on the subject.
I think it was suggested that a large expenditure should be made which was not necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No expenditure, so far as I know, has been recommended by the Lighthouse Board.

I wish to bring up the case of Margaree island,, which is distant three miles from the shore. There is a lighthouse on it and a fishing station, and I think that it would come within the purview of this policy. I should like to see a telephone station there. There is a line of telephone along the coast of Inverness, and this is a very important station. The lighthouse keeper has great difficulty in landing during several months. I submit to the minister that the establishment of a telephone station there would be a great convenience to the fishermen.

The harbour of Kouchibouguac in my province is a port of call during the whole season for fishing and trading vessels, but there is no communication by telephone or telegraph. If the present system could be extended some eight or ten miles along the shore, it would be a great convenience to that section of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Whom does the line belong to?
It is operated by the Government.

Is it the intention of
the department to take over the pilot system in the Maritime Provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The system under which
the pilotage service on the St. Lawrence has been taken over and placed under the authority of the minister .has worked admirably, and there is a good deal to be said in favour of applying the same system at Halifax, St. John, Sydney, on the Pacific coast, and at other places where there are pilot commissions. I should like to have the matter discussed some time and obtain the views of gentlemen who are interested in it. Of course, opposition to the plan will come from certain quarters. I am disposed to think, however, without expressing a matured opinion, that a change along the lines of the system prevailing on the St. Lawrence would be a benefit to the shipping interests. I have had the matter in mind for several years, but 'since the outbreak of war it has been hard to get time to deal with questions of that kind. I hope some time to formulate a plan and subinit it to Parliament.

In the Auditor General's Report, the minister will find mention of two wharves, one at Grand Narrows, Victoria county, and the other at Grand Narrows, Cape Breton county. Victoria county is on the west side of Grand Narrows and Cape Breton is on the east side. These two wharves are utilized in receiving and discharging freight from the Intercolonial railway. Nothing is charged on either of them and, under the old order of things, the same applied at Baddeck wharf. Since the Conservatives came in, however, they have charged over $100 at that wharf. I think it should be placed in the same category with the Grand Narrows wharf, at which no wharfage is collected.

New vessel to replace the Maisonneuve*

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is a vessel of composite construction, being built at the Government yards at Sorel to take the place of a boat of the same name which has been condemned by the inspectors as unserviceable. The cost will be $30,000. We spent last year $17,861, and this vote is for the purpose of completing the vessel, which, we think, will be in commission this month.

Is she to be used on
the St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Maisonneuve will be
used on the Ottawa river for the lighthouse service, doing the work formerly carried on by the old boat.
Amount required for rebuilding of Scout, $12,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Scout was built at
Cardinal, Ontario, seventeen years ago. It is a wooden vessel and was employed in the lighthouse and buoy service in the upper St. Lawrence river. Quite extensive repairs were found to be necessary to the hull. We thought at first that we should have to have a new boat, but careful inspection demonstrated the fact that the boat could be repaired and made serviceable for a good many years yet. The repairs were made at Kingston.
Has the hon. gentleman any further details concerning the settlement of the strike at the Sorel shipyard?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The strike is settled. The men are all at woik to-day, and peace and harmony prevail. -
What were the conditions of the settlement?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We increased the pay in some cases where we thought increases were deserved, and some of the men who, we thought, acted very improperly, were asked to stand aside. From what I can judge by the representations made to me, the great bulk of the men in the yard Eeel that there was no justification for the extreme measures to which the men resorted, because the department was considering the whole question and was prepared to deal fairly and properly with it. We had two officials there and they said: We are prepared to look into the matter and to make a report, and in consequence of the changed condition of affairs, in regard to the wages to be paid, we are authorized by the minister to say that the department will pay them. This was not satisfactory

to all the men and some of them shut down the machinery. When that occurred, I gave orders to close the works because I did not think we should be taken by the throat in that manner, but I learned the next day from many of the men that they deeply regretted what had taken place and that they were willing to return again and were quite sure that the department would give them every consideration.

Were any increases
given?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Increases were given where they were warranted.
Did you give the men all that they asked for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Has any decision been arrived at by the department in regard to the land where the department is operating there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You mean the McCarthy estate?

Yes. Has there been any settlement made with the estate? Some years ago a lease was entered into with the McCarthy estate; that lease has expired, and I believe the department is still a tenant although there is no renewal of lease with the estate. I understand that the Government intend to purchase the land. If a settlement has been arrived at, what amount has been fixed, and what terms generally have' been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We were not able to come to an agreement with the McCarthy estate. We felt that in view of the lease we had entered into, the amount they wished for the property was entirely in excess of its value; we could not agree to pay them the amount they wanted and they could not agree to take the amount we were willing to pay them, and the result was that we have undertaken to expropriate the property through the Exchequer Court.
What is the margin of difference between the offer of the -Government and the amount required by the estate?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My recollection is that the margin is very large.	[DOT]

Are the expropriation
proceedings going on?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The matter is in the hands of the Justice Department, and I presume proceedings will be taken in due course.

Has the case been
entered?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know. I have
not had the matter before me for some time, but my recollection is that we instructed the Department of Justice to take proceedings in the matter of expropriation; I think the papers are filed which would vest us with the control of the property, and I think the Department of Justice have taken proceedings to have the Exchequer Court place a value on it.
Mr. LEMfEUX: I hold no brief for the estate except that I happen to know casually the little difference of opinion there is between the department and the estate. One of the McCarthy's was a class-mate of mine, and that is how I happen to know of the matter. I believe the Government has taken the proper course in referring the matter to the Exchequer Court because the department must come to terms some way or another on account of the fact that you occupy the grounds which belong to the estate and which are very valuable, in fact, the department could not do otherwise than to have the shipyards there. The last time I had occasion to look into this matter, the department refused to agree to the price, but were still occupying the property, and the estate drew rent from the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Under the lease they were entitled to $1,200 a year.
Yes, but when the lease expired they refused to renew it, and for some time there was correspondence between the estate and the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The lease was1 a very peculiar one. One contention was that tite lease was practically perpetual; that it never expired, and that as long as we chose to hold the property and pay $1,200 a year, we had the right to do so, and we kept tendering that $1,200 a year. After, however, having taken the advice of the Department of Justice, and having considered the matter, we decided it was better for all concerned to expropriate and thus get the absolute right to the property.
What about the marine railway at Sorel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not heard of it for many years.	^

In connection with
the construction pf the steamer Maison-neuve, where does the department get the

engines and boilers for steamers that are constructed in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The boilers that we use at Sorel we make ourselves. I do not know where the engines for the Maisenneuve came fr.om, but my impression is that they were built by a private firm after tenders had been called for. There are a number of private firms at Sorel constructing engines.
In regard to vessels generally that aTe built in the department or for the department, is it possible to have satisfactory engines constructed in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: ^es, we have found that to be the case.
The theory used tp be that we could not get satisfactory engines or boilers except in England?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The information from my officials, who know more about the matter than I do, is that the engines we have had built in Canada for our boats have been satisfactory.

For quite a while,
the boilers for the boats that were built in Canada were so constructed that it was impossible to use Canadian coal. The boilers used in connection with these steamers have no difficulty in that regard? 1

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We use Nova. Scotia coal altogether in connection with the St. Lawrence ship-channel work and with all our steamers.
Scientific institutions - Meteorological service, etc., $201,793.

What is the increase
due to?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is due to increases in salaries. The salaries are small, and we are giving the ordinary statutory increases of $50 or $100.
Where are these stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The head meteorological station is at Toronto, and that is where most of the expense is. The head man is Sir Frederick Stupart, and he has a staff of officials at Toronto. There are other stations at Victoria, St. John, Quebec, Moosejaw, Edmonton, Halifax, Fredericton, Montreal, Winnipeg Woodstock and Sherbrooke. There are also telegraph stations at Vancouver, Kingston, Chatham, Port Arthur, Charlottetown, Sydney, Yarmouth, Atlin, Swift Current Prince Rupert, Dawson and other places all over Canada.
Does this item covet the expense of the telegraph service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Is it necessary to have this telegraph service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is necessary to collect the information in order that the probabilities may be sent out.	[DOT]
You do not own the telegraph lines, but simply pay for this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We pay for the service. The station at Bermuda costs $375. The station at Triangle Island, at the entrance to Prince Rupert, $250; Regina, $240. There are also stations at White River, Father Point, Sable Island, and places like that. The total cost of the telegraph stations is $17,000.
Are reports wired from Sir Frederick Stupart's office all over Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Sir Frederick Stupart's
office collects all the information, and then sends out reports as to the weather probabilities in the lake region, the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and so on.
What are the probabilities for the next political storm?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have got to get the different elements together first, before I can tell you that.
Do storm drums come under this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
I have a little grievance which I want to bring to the minister's attention. Who is the man in charge of the storm drum at Grand Etang?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: His name is not here, but he gets $60 a year.
Are these yearly appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not necessarily so; they are made from time to time.

These are very important stations to us, as they fournish a great deal of information that is of vast benefit to the fishermen particularly. A man by the name of Cormier was placed in charge of the storm drum at Grand Etang some seven or eight years ago. He gave a first class service in every respect. He was in poor circumstances and in poor health,

and my information is that he has been dismissed and another man appointed in his place. It is very important that I should know who his successor is, because I have a word or two to say in regard to this service, which has saved perhaps more lives than any other.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I should be very glad to give my hon. friend the information, but I have not got it here.

I think possibly I have the information myself. I have a very strong impression that this man was dismissed on account of municipal politics. It is a disastrous condition of affairs if the service of this country is to be prostituted at the instance of political demagogues scattered all over the country. The position that this man occupied was of very great importance to our fishermen, and he gave a first class service. We may have a municipal election again next fall and this man's successor, if he does not vote the right way, may be dismissed and some one else be appointed in his place. In my judgment the dismissal of this man is about as small a piece of business as I have heard of since I came to this House. I do not think the minister knows anything at all about it because he has too great a sense of fairness to allow anything like that to take place. I have no doutot that some under-strappers who control some portions of his department are responsible for this dismissal. This may be a small thing-the minister says the salary is only $60, tout I can tell him that the service is worth a great deal more than that to the fishermen who are dependent upon the notices sent out from this station. It is a very Tough coast down there, and these storm drums were put up possibly at my instance, and have given excellent service, tout if the whole machinery is going to be put in the hands of local politicians I am sorry the storm drums were eveT put up. Would the minister investigate this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will look into it.
If the minister finds that this man gave perfect satisfaction, will he restore him? It is not often I make a request, but I feel that a great injustice has been done in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman must
not press me too hard.

I have great
regard for the minister's word, and if he
says he will replace this man, I shall be content.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will look into the matter.
Marine hospitals, including grants to Institutes assisting sailors, $75,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The amount we spent last year up to the 31st of March was $57,540. There are some items for April that will have to be added to that. The amounts that have been spent for the last six years since 1910-1911 are resepectivtely $54,000, $52,000, $54,000, $65,000, $64,000 and $57,000. Owing to the increasing cost of living the hospitals have found it necessary to increase the per diem rate for hospital treatment at certain points. Arrangements are made in ports where there is a well-established public hospital for the sailors to receive treatment at a per diem rate. The rate used to -be $1 a day, but the hospitals have had to increase that to $1.50. That includes nursing, attendance and everything else required. The hospitals represent that there has been a great increase not only 'in the price of food but in drugs and hospital supplies. It is expected that this amount will cover all expenditures during the coming year.
How is this vote administered at Canso?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The resident doctor there is Dr. A. McGarry.
How are patients provided for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is no hospital there, and patients are sent to a private house, under an arrangement made.
What about the marine hospital at Point Tupper, closed some years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the patients there in need of treatment are sent to the hospital at Sydney.
Who is the marine doctor at the strait of Canso? Dr. McLeod,, of Hawkesbury was the physician there, but he was dismissed by this Government, and Dr. McKenzie, of Port Mulgrave, was appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The incumbent of the hospital having died, Dr. McKenzie has been appointed temporarily in his place.
Has the minister had a request from Canso in regard to an increase of the expenses there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have had correspondence about the matter, and have agreed to pay an increased amount.
Is it on account of the increased cost of drugs?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, but we have to pay more to the house to which sailors are sent, just as we have to pay increased rates to the different hospitals.

I understand that the request from the medical officer was for an increase on account of the greater cost of drugs, and I heard a fear expressed that the service might be discontinued unless the minister paid attention to that request.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Dr. McGarry is paid $375 a year, and out of this supplies his own medicines.
What is the minister going to do about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If we increase the amount paid to one doctor on account of the increased cost of drugs, we could hardly refuse to make that increase general, because it is not in Canso alone that drugs are more costly. Before I increase their pay all over the country, I should have to give the matter very careful consideration.

At Canso there is no
doctor available except Dr. McGarry. There is a doctor at Hazel Hill, but he is employed by the cable company and is not at liberty to attend to sailors. . If Dr. McGarry withdrew from the service, it would be difficult to replace him. I think it is true that he is not getting enough, particularly since the cost of drugs has become so great. There are usually quite a number of calls upon him. I would like the minister to look into this matter and see if the physician's request is not a reasonable one.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There may be exceptional circumstances at Canso, as the hon. member seems to think. I will look into it.

Who is the port physician
at St. Peter's?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Dr. J. A. McDonald.
What is his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is $250.

Is that the salary at which
he was appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know.
Do these doctors report the number of patients they attend?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, they report quarterly.
By looking at that report the minister could see what service is rendemd by the port physician at Canso?
Who is the port physician at Cheticamp?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is Dr. P. J. L. Fiset.
Is he permanently appointed, and is he paid a fixed amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
I see by the
Auditor General's Report that Dr. Fiset received $125.75 and Dr. Lablanc $115.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The change was made since the report from which the hon. gentleman is quoting was made. At one time there were two doctors there acting as port physicians, and each making a charge for the work actually performed by him, with the result that we paid a pretty large sum for the service. Now we have an arrangement with Dr. Fiset by which the whole serivce is performed for $300.

Where the port physician
is not available and a.vessel comes in with a sick mariner aboard, and another doctor has to be called in, how are the fees provided for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a fairly well established rule. Unless the port physician is able to give satisfactory reasons why he was not available, and why he did not arrange with somebody else to conduct his business for him while he was away, we pay the other doctor and deduct the amount from the salary of the port physician.

It appears to me that the fact that thp regular port physician is not on the ground to render medical service ought to be a sufficient reason for the department deducting the amount of the service from his salary. I do not think that any question ought to arise as to the reasons why the services of the port physician are not available. There are cases where hardships are occasioned when mariners pay sick mariners' dues. If a mariner is sick and the port physician is absent he will be obliged to call in another physician. Is it the invariable practice of the department to pay for the services of the other physician and deduct from the salary of the regular physician?

Mr. HAZEN i I believe that is practically the course pursued in almost every case. There may be some exceptional reason why it would not be just tor the department to do that but in the great majority of cases that is done. As a rule, there is generally an arrangement among the doctors to take care of each other's cases during the absence of any one of them.

A short time ago Capt. Poirier came into the port of Arichat very ill and he sent for the port physician, Dr. P. A. LeBlanc. For some reason or other, the port physician did not answer to the call. Captain Poirier was obliged to secure the services of another doctor, the doctor rendered his bill to the captain and the captain naturally looks to the department to indemnify him. I would like to know if that is one of the cases in which the minister would think that the port physician ought to be charged with the fees of the other practitioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not had an opportunity of looking into the facts. They ought to be submitted to us and then we could come to a decision about them.
Do I understand that Dr. McLeod has been permanently appointed as port physician at Hawkesbury?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, he is acting temporarily.	,
He takes the cases as they come along?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes; under an arrangement with him and we pay him.
Does he look after the cases at Mulgrave as well as at Hawkesbury?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
How much was received for sick mariners' dues last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: That covers the whole expenditure of this item and a little more?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It more than covers it.
So that we are not losing anything on this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
I understand that there is a considerable amount to the credit of the fund for past years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I think that is a reason why the minister should be a little more liberal with the port physicians. The fact that they are pressed down to the lowest amount is not a good thing for the service. The natural result is that the doctor who only gets $200 or $300 a year for this service does not take much interest in it and the sailor suffers. If the minister would look into the particular case of each port and ascertain the work that is done, and whether it is necessary to give a living wage to the doctor who is doing it, it would be better for the service, and it would give a fair chance to the men who are being attended. Sailors are apt to be poorly looked after if the department is not paying the parties who are looking after them fairly, or as they would be paid by outside people for the same service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is one reason why we endeavour, wherever we can, to get the sailors to go to the hospitals.

I am speaking now about places where there are no hospitals. T have drawn the attention of the minister to a ease of hardship that occurred at the port of Canso in years gone by, partly because there was no proper place at which to attend sick sailors when they came in. They could not get proper attention because they had to go to some boarding house. If they come in sick with a contagious disease the appliances are very poor, and it could hardly be expected that a doctor would do his best work for the fee that he is getting at a port like Canso, where so many seamen and fishermen from the Banks come in, to say nothing of the medical requirements of the locality. There is a bright young doctor at Mulgrave by the name of Dr. Breen, a very capable young man, and I thought that at the time when Dr. McKenzie's death took place he would be his successor, as he took up Dr. McKenzie's work in Mulgrave and carried it on. He would have been the natural person to appoint for this service, and if my hon. friend is looking for a man to take the place permanently he could not do better than appoint Dr. Breen, who is at Mulgrave, who is well capable of doing the work arid who is trusted by everybody.

This is an occasion when I have much pleasure on congratulating the minister on making the selection of Dr. McLeod, because he is situated at the port of Hawkesbury, most of

the shipping is done there and I have no dou'bt that the minister will see his way clear to make the appointment permanent and leave Dr. McLeod where he is. They will have to come over from Mulgrave to Hawke^bury, because it is the main shipping point.
Who is the medical officer at Cape Tormentine?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Dr. Allen.
He left there some time ago and he has since died.	.

speechtext:

speechtext:
We will let the item stand,
with the understanding that it is open to hon. members to discuss any questions on it, as there are a number not present to-night who are interested in these Estimates. I might say to my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that in accordance with his suggestion of last session I propose, on taking up the Fisheries Estimates, to make a general statement on the progress of the fisheries. I had perhaps better not start that to-night.
Progress reported.
